speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last night on "The Journal" television program the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) indicated that a portion of the Western Development Fund would be used to finance housing for Indians living in western Canada. On November 3, 1982, Senator Jack Austin confirmed in the Senate that this expenditure was in fact national in scope. Like the payment of funds to farmers for losses as a result of the Soviet grain embargo, this is another example of how the federal Government is trying to delude the people of western Canada into believing that a fund for western development actually exists. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That this House asks the Minister of Finance to get his facts straight concerning the Western Development Fund and that he admit that money from this Fund will be spent across Canada, not just in the West as promised.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in his question, the Hon. Member has shown that he is a little confused about the Government's objective in giving this mandate to its new holding company. The Hon. Member wondered whether the purpose was to transfer funds from certain corporations that are making a profit to others that are less profitable. The Government's objective is, first of all, to provide for stricter management of shares held by the Canadian government in the Canada Development Corporation, and also to provide for stricter management of other commercial corporations that are wholly owned by the Government of Canada. The Government also intends to offer opportunities to private companies that might be interested in a joint venture with the government, both with respect to ownership and management. Thus, by diversifying ownership of companies and by increasing management control through the expertise that will be provided by the people heading this new corporation, we will improve the financial well-being of corporations that may be experiencing difficulties, and we will be giving the private sector an opportunity to obtain an interest in corporations that are financially more attractive.
Madam Speaker, I do not quite understand where the Minister of National Revenue comes in on this particular topic.

Madam Speaker, the former President of the Treasury Board, in the first speech he made after he became the Minister, said that he was going to follow the policies proposed by the Government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to privatize Crown corporations. Since then nothing has happened, even though there have been many opportunities.
Can the Prime Minister give any assurances, such as giving specific deadlines of when companies will be privatized, or is this CDIC just another example of the same old Liberal shell game of shuffling mistakes around to make it appear things are being done, but in fact the whole process is simply one of hiding gross errors?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):

Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to apologize to the Hon. Member and explain why I rose in the House just now. The reason is that the minister responsible for this corporation sits in the Senate, and thus the Prime Minister asked me to
answer in the House on behalf of this new corporation, namely, the Canada Development Investment Corporation. I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that in view of his experience in business and the capital markets, he ought to know that it would not necessarily be very wise from the financial point to set definite dates for the partial or total privatization of a company that is owned by the Government of Canada. He knows perfectly well that where diversification of ownership or privatization of a company is concerned, the government must try to get the best possible return on these assets, and that in such cases, it must consider market conditions and wait until those conditions and any offers made have been assessed in terms of the resulting return on the investment made by all Canadians in these corporations.
Madam Speaker, I think the translation of that is yes, it is the same old Liberal shell game.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. As he knows, the 88 Trade Ministers are now meeting in Geneva for the first time in nine years under the terms of the GATT Agreement, and the meeting is chaired by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, our fugitive from Finance. That Minister said at Geneva, and I quote him, "Protectionist policies, by obstructing internaional trade, are accumulatively destructive of employment," meaning jobs, "and, by undermining efficiency exacerbate inflation," meaning increased inflation. Is this the Government's policy and belief? If so, will the Government now eliminate its own protective policy which it has adopted and that we have seen evidence of in recent months?
Did the Government, in preparing for this very important meeting consult, with the U.S. Government? Have we developed a joint strategy with the United States, and are we working with the U.S. in that Government's attempt to liberalize world trade?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in terms of consultation, this subject has come up at least at the two most recent Summits which Canadian representatives attended, first at Versailles and then in Montebello. On both of those occasions Canada was one of the strongest voices in fighting against any tendency toward protectionism.
We all know the evils that the beggar-my-neighbour policies caused in the 1930s, and I think it is fair to say that the industrialized countries, particularly the Summit Seven, are very concerned about the possibility of a return to that type of protectionism. That is the role the Secretary of State for External Affairs is taking as Chairman of the Conference, but that is more particularly the role which the Minister responsible for international trade will be playing as head of the Canadian delegation in the Geneva meetings.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister said that we have been a strong voice for the elimination of protectionism, and for free trade. Is our Government going to act, in addition to having a strong voice, because if the Government acts differently than it says, then that is hypocrisy and it does not persuade anyone? In the future is this to be the guiding principle and will it be acted on by the Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister did not answer my query as to whether we have developed a joint strategy with the United States. If not, are we trying to develop a joint strategy with the European Economic Community with whom he has a contractual arrangement? Is that contractual arrangement worth anything, because today people are taking a very protective attitude at Geneva? Are we co-ordinating and do we have a joint strategy with the United States? If not, do we have a joint strategy with the European Economic Community? Will the Prime Minister tell us whether we are going to act to eliminate protectionism and help free trade, in addition to voicing that principle which is so often not observed and breached?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in terms of a joint strategy I thought I had indicated in my reply that the Seven Summit countries and, indeed, the European Economic Community representatives, tried to establish such a strategy, and that Canada was part of it. Naturally within that over-all strategy of fighting collectively against protectionist trends, Canada's strategy is mainly to protect itself. I discussed these matters with the European leaders whom I met last week, the German Chancellor, the French President and Prime Minister. We are aware of some general willingness to act together in this, but I would not say that the strategy will be the same in all cases for everyone.
In so far as lowering our protectionist barriers is concerned,
I would be the first to admit that there are some protectionist barriers erected by Canada in the case of some very soft industries, like textiles, the leather industry, and the clothing industry. This is true, I believe, for just about every industrialized country. Certainly it is true in the case of textiles for the U.S. to a much more massive degree than for Canada. We are all sensitive to this reality and that is why Canada, in particular, is trying to phase out even those protectionist measures. We hope we will be successful, but I will not pretend that we
November 25, 1982

can overnight withdraw all protection to these particular industries and still indicate our concern for the Canadian economy.
I do not believe seriously that Hon. Members opposite would propose that all quotas be lifted immediately in those particular areas. If such is their policy, I would challenge them to make it clear. If such is not their policy, they are just as protectionist as I am, which is to say not very much.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister responsible for International Trade. The United States International Trade Commission has found that imported Canadian lumber may be injurious to the U.S. lumber industry. speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as far as this question is concerned, the Government of Canada, in co-operation with the provincial governments and especially with industry, has already notified the American authorities that we do not agree with the preliminary finding which alleges that a subsidy was attached to provincial royalties with respect to logging operations. A joint representation has been made to the American authorities. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has mentioned the matter directly to the U.S. Secretary of State, Mr. Schultz. Last week, when the Minister of State for International Trade was visiting Washington, he, too, mentioned this to the American Secretary of State for Trade, and we are continuing our joint lobby with the provinces and industry to prevent this preliminary finding regarding a possible subsidy from going any further, but in any case, the U.S. Administration will not be making a decision much earlier than March or April.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister for his encouraging report. I am sure the Minister is as aware as 1 am of the very serious effect that this major export market has on the Canadian lumber industry, particularly in the Atlantic provinces and in British Columbia.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It relates to Canadian atomic veterans and civilians who have petitioned and appealed to the Government to

November 25, 1982
Oral Questions
undertake a comprehensive medical study to attempt to determine whether the health problems they are experiencing relate to their exposure to radiation. The Government made a commitment last June to fund the study and that it would be released wihtin six months.
It now appears that the study has not been approved and, in the event it is approved, it will not go forward until January. subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, November 18, consideration of the Motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 spoke on this Bill for about ten minutes on November 18 and I am certainly very happy to have the opportunity to say a few more words.
I started to review the purpose of indexing. Indexing was brought in in order to enable people on fixed incomes to meet rising costs due to the increasing cost of essential food, clothing and shelter, and general inflation. They both have an effect on those on fixed incomes. Therefore, in order to permit a person at least to maintain a reasonable standard of living, indexing was invoked and made law in the country. If the purpose of indexing in the first place was to make sure that those on fixed incomes were going to be able to continue to live, warm their houses and provide clothes for themselves and their dependants, then I would like the Hon. Minister to tell me how these people are going to meet their needs if it is not continued.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I recall some time ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stating that all these people had to do was change their priorities. People who have large incomes, or inheritances, such as the Prime Minister himself, or those receiving other pensions, are quite able to change priorities. But I want to say that a large number of pensioners, just about half of them according to the Minister's own statement, are in a class where they will be affected by this deindexing, and out of that group 1 suppose there is no more than 10 per cent who are in the heavy financial areas.
There are a lot of Canadians past the age of 65 who are still working and have not accepted the old age pension in spite of its universality or the CPP, even though they have paid into it for several years. When you consider the number who are not pensioners at all, then that increases the number of pensioners who really need indexing.
Now, I am not arguing in favour of those who do not need indexing to have a reasonable standard of living. Not at all; they should bear their share of the costs of running the country. But to place the mass of old age pensioners in that group is not fair at all. I suppose every Hon. Member in this House who has helped pensioners fill in forms or look after their problems knows that a very large number of those pensioners are just on the edge of getting GIS. Every time there is an increase in the indexation, it brings in a few more people because the amount they are allowed to earn goes up. Now that amount will go up at a slower rate than it did before. Consequently, there will still be that group which is left to live entirely off the basic pension, many of them with practically no other income. If they are not getting GIS, they must have other income.
Those who have any experience with this at all know that the GIS Is based on the income of a year ago, not the current year. People may have secured money from relatives or other sources a year ago, but many of these people are now having a tough time; they no longer have any other sources of income, and they are now going to have to stay in that group for another two years because the pension they receive is not going to rise and their income is going to go down. As the basic income is cut, those who are on basic pension are going to receive less money.
A program put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare shows that the amount of money coming from this source in 1983 will be $90 million. In other words, $90 million is taken out of the income of pensioners in this country. Many of them cannot afford it; they need that money themselves. In 1984 it will amount to $150 million. That amount of money will remain in Government coffers and will not go into the marketplace. Pensioners spend their money, and over the two years that is $240 million which is not going to get into the pockets of pensioners and out into the economy. Many of them can ill afford to have this happen.

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I was interested to hear a few moments ago the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) say that the Government wanted to be more human in the reform of Parliament. Well, fine, Mr. Speaker; but I want the Government to be more human with regard to its treatment of the senior citizens of this country and those who are in need. If the Government is going to be more human it can show it by withdrawing Bill C-131 and Bill C-133. Bill C-131 alone will deny the $240 million which rightfully, under present legislation, would go into the pockets of the pensioners of this country, and from there into the stores where it would help those who are trying to stay in business. The $240 million over the years 1983 and 1984 comes under Bill C-131, not Bill C-133 which deals with supplementary retirement benefits and is almost a companion Bill to Bill C-131. It is hard to discuss one without discussing the other.
In looking at Bill C-131, Mr. Speaker, the first two words are very revealing, particularly with regard to the actions of this Government. The bill starts out by saying in Clause 1(5):
Notwithstanding anything-
That is how this Government operates. Notwithstanding anything, if the Government wants to do something, it does not matter whether it is human or right or wrong; it does not matter who is going to pay the bill or suffer because of it. Notwithstanding anything, the Government is going to do it, as Hon. Members opposite now say they are determined to pass this Bill notwithstanding anything-notwithstanding the fact that some of their own Members have publicly said that they cannot support this Bill. I admire them for that, but I will admire them more if they will stand up and tell the world when the vote is being taken that they cannot support this Bill. That will be the proof of the pudding, because talk is easy and talk is cheap.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Well, shut your mouth.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Well, you should stand up and express your views. At least I am not afraid to say what I think and what my constituents think.
Notwithstanding anything, this Government will be doing a lot of things, including desecrating and destroying a beautiful park in Banff. Notwithstanding anything, whether it is right or wrong, the Government is quite prepared to do that. I still question the Government's authority to reduce indexation under Bill C-133, because that money was paid by the participants themselves into a separate fund. The Government has a contract with the senior citizens of this country but it does not have any hesitation about breaking that contract. Yet the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) said he could not break a contract. Why he ever made such a ridiculous contract involving parkland is more than I will ever know. Why did he not check into it before he signed the contract, before permitting the permit to be issued, before allowing the land to be transferred? That is what a proper Minister would properly have done.
When I asked the former minister of finance a few months ago what authority he had to stop indexing the pensions of
superannuates, he said, "Well, we will get the authority; we may not have it but we will get it". And there is the Bill that is going to do it. The Government simply changed the contract in mid-stream.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough in a country like Canada. If we are going to break contracts with senior citizens, those who cannot defend themselves, and then refuse to break contracts with favourite sons, well, it is a pretty bad situation. It tells the people what is going on in this country.
Dealing for a minute or so with why this Bill should not be passed, inflation is now 10.4 per cent. Senior citizens have nothing to do with inflation but the Government has. The Government's wild expenditures over the last few years have been a major cause of inflation. The Government kept telling the people to tighten their belts but kept increasing its own expenditures. Even this year it is increasing the deficit. The Government asks everyone to cut back to what it calls six and five, but is the Government cutting back? Why does it not cut out the waste in Government before it starts taking $240 million out of the pockets of senior citizens who are on the basic pension? Many of these people are having a difficult time making ends meet. Even the increase in pension through indexing does not meet the increase in their costs, many of which are directly due to the policies of the Government.
In 1982 the average increase in the cost of energy all over the country was 16.4 per cent. That did not come about through any action taken by senior citizens, or anyone else for that matter; it came about because the Government was money hungry. Every petroleum tax possible was increased and so was the tax on heating oil. In Alberta alone, in one case $1.85 of the $2 increase in the cost of energy went to the federal Government in taxes.
The Government now calls on people to help it fight inflation but, Mr. Speaker, the Government aggravated inflation and added to it. Senior citizens had no say in that but now the Government is asking them to cut back or go without. Why does it not appeal to the group of senior citizens who can get by without Old Age Security and the Canada Pension? The Government knows the income of every person who applies for the old age pension and Canada Pension. It now claims that the Canada Pension is not affected by this measure because citizens have contributed to it. Well, Mr. Speaker, the superannuates contributed as well under a different type of arrangement, but the Government is not hesitating to say it will cut off some of the money in that fund. It is not going to touch the Canada Pension-and I do not think it should-but neither should it touch the indexing of the superannuates. How is someone who does not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement going to meet the increase in the cost of energy, for instance? The Prime Minister has told them to change their priorities, to turn down the heat and not use so much light. A lot of them are doing their utmost to comply, but it is not easy.
November 25, 1982

The last time I spoke on this subject in the Elouse, Mr. Speaker, I spoke about a senior citizen and his wife whom 1 visited. He was wearing a heavy sweater and she was wearing a heavy kimono. For the thirty minutes I was in the home I left my overcoat on and I can tell you 1 was cold, but they were trying to co-operate with the Government. They do not receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement because their income is just above the qualifying line. In effect, the Government is now going to take the money that should go into their pockets while telling them to change their priorities.
The 16.4 per cent increase in the cost of energy is largely due to the actions of the Government and its hunger for money. The price of clothing has increased by 4.9 per cent. Now that we are approaching winter people must have warm clothes, but how are they going to get them? As the Prime Minister says, they will have to change their priorities- perhaps go without food. Sometimes a male senior citizen is unable to get around so his wife has to go out and do their business. She must have warm clothes or she will freeze to death in our cold winters. But how is she going to get them?
I am speaking of people on fixed incomes, many of whom are barely getting by. Some people have to apply for welfare because they just cannot get by on the basic pension. That is a great tribute to this country with its tremendous wealth, I must say! People who have spent a lifetime building the country are being told that the indexing is to be removed from their pension but that they can apply for welfare. That is the only way many of them would be able to change their priorities, as the Prime Minister has suggested. Of course, he can change his priorities any time he likes, but people who have worked and laboured throughout the years cannot all do that. The price of food has increased and, of course, people have to eat. Does the Prime Minister want them to change that priority as well? Perhaps they will have to live on pork and beans entirely, but even the price of pork and beans has increased.
Statistics show that in 1982 the price of energy increased by 16.4 per cent, clothes by 4.9 per cent and food by 6.5 per cent. That is almost 27 per cent in total, Mr. Speaker, Now the Government proposes to cut the indexing of pensions and wants pensioners to get by on that. They might get by, but it will be pretty tough and it is a disgrace to the country.
Some historian said that we evaluate a country by the way it treats its disabled, its handicapped and its senior citizens. Our senior citizens have spent a lifetime building the country and in many cases have contributed to other causes to the point that they have little left for themselves. Those aged 65 and over came through the Depression and now the Government is threatening to cut more off their incomes, as if they did not contribute enough in the hungry thirties.
A good motto for the Government to use in the next election would be "Notwithstanding anything, we will do what we like if we have a majority. We will not listen to what the Opposition says."
As a matter of interest, Mr. Speaker, there is not one Minister in the House. I suppose I might just as well be talking out in the backwoods for all the good it does in this place.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Ministers do not remain to hear what the Opposition has to say although they often complain that the Opposition has nothing to offer. I do not know of a provincial Government in the country in the last 20 years where the Minister responsible for legislation did not remain in the House to listen to debate on his or her Bill. I know a lot of Provinces where the Premier and Ministers spend a good deal of time in the House and stay there all the time when something concerning their Department is being discussed. After question period here, however, it often happens that there is no Minister present, or sometimes only one or two. There is a handful of faithfuls opposite who are there pretty nearly all the time. People are rapidly catching on. This will not go on forever.
The Minister says that the Government needs the money, that it needs $240 million. First it should cut out some of its needless waste. There is no need for the Government to send a public servant to Paris to study for a year. If anyone else in the country wants to go to Paris to study, he or she has to pay for it. I would imagine that it is a wonderful place to study. I would like to go there myself; I would have liked to go there a few years ago but I could never afford it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It is possible on Ed Clark's salary.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes. If one gets into the right Department and gets to know the Prime Minister and the Minister, he can do it, notwithstanding anything. Whoever wrote this Bill sure knew what he was writing-"nothwithstanding anything". The Government sent this man Clark to study in Paris, I suppose at the Sorbonne. I do not know how much it will cost. He is getting his wages and enough to live handsomely on in Paris. That could have gone quite a way toward reducing the deficit or eliminating the need for $240 million being taken out of the pockets of the senior citizens of the country.
Notwithstanding anything, if a person is the right one, he can go to the Riviera, of all places, for a year at Government expense. If she wanted to learn French, why did she not learn it in Quebec? There are excellent teachers there; it was not necessary to go to the Riviera. In fact, she could learn it right here in Ottawa as many other public servants are doing, at their own expense. In many cases the Government pays the cost of the instruction; in many cases it does not. Some people are paying for their own instruction, but the Government can send one person, the favourite daughter, the favourite of the Prime Minister, to the Riviera.
There must be $100,000 spent per year on these two people in terms of wages, subsistence, air fare and everything else in the Riviera and in Paris. If that is not waste, I do not know what waste is. Then the Government takes $240 million out of the pockets of senior citizens. It takes money out of the pockets of superannuates, people who have spent part of their lives improving the country, or R.C.M.P. being shot at. What about members of the Armed Forces who spent part of their lives on the battlefields of the world, or public servants who spent

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
countless hours trying to work out the best policies for Canada? We will break the contract with them if we pass Bill C-133.
If this is the type of policy the country is going to have, we need a new government. It is almost the last straw when the Government starts picking on people who cannot defend themselves.
Telephone bills are up. Some people ask what right they have to have telephones. "They are senior citizens living on the basic pension and they are not supposed to have telephones", one chap said to me. "Why do they want telephones?" They want telephones because they are human beings. For many of them it is the only way they can talk to other people. Because their health will not permit them to go out, they have to phone for their groceries and everything. I could take you, Mr. Speaker, into some of the homes of people in that category. Telephone costs have risen. How will senior citizens be able to meet this increased cost, especially when the Government starts cutting down their pensions by cutting their indexing?
Water rates have risen. They have to have water. I suppose some smart public servants, speaking on behalf of the Government, maybe those who prepared this legislation, may say, "They do not need to take baths; let them have their cup of water a day but they do not need to take baths." Some of them are now only taking baths once or twice a month simply because they cannot afford the water bills. I know pensioners who wanted to water their gardens last summer but did not dare do it because they could not afford it.
Sales taxes are up, and the Government introduces a Bill which puts an excise tax on gas, making the price of food go up. It is one of the most terrible things the Government has ever done because it affects almost all the people of Canada, not only farmers. It adversely affects farmers because some of them cannot afford fertilizer. What will that do to the land? In time it will hurt the land and hurt production. The other day a knowledgeable farmer in Alberta said that many farmers this year could not afford fertilizer because of the excise tax. The Government is putting everything out of reach, and we wonder how people will live.
Another point in connection with this Bill is the overpayments. I wish the Government could understand the agony created in the hearts of our senior citizens when it sends them cheques and then discovers six months later it has sent them too much. The pensioners have spent the money but still have not met all their needs, and then they receive letters which frighten them because they are told that they have to pay back the money. From where will they get it? It was the Government's mistake in sending the money out. If someone deliberately tries to defraud the Government, then let him take his punishment. In many of these cases it is the Government's bookkeeping, computer and calculations that were wrong. When the pensioners received the money, they had every right to expect that it was theirs.
I see the Speaker rising because my time is up, but I want to say that the Bill should be defeated roundly. When we defeat it, I hope we also defeat the Government.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-131. First I want to say what good things may be said about the Bill, and then I shall come to the "but". I am afraid it will not take very long to come to the "but".
The ostensible purpose of the measure is to assist in getting our economic house in order. It is pretty hard to find fault with this laudable aim. Surely it is and must be our most immediate and pressing task, as well as our highest priority. Mr. Speaker will find no disagreement with that role on this side of the House; indeed, we have been pressing the same on the Government for some time now.
This was the aim of the budget of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) of December, 1979, two and a half years before the Party opposite noticed that there was a problem. Or at least, to give it the benefit of every doubt, before it acknowledged publicly that the world would be unfolding better than it seemed to be at the moment.
How much of the time of the House is taken up with piecemeal band-aid attempts to remedy the earlier sins of omission and commission of that gaggle of happy fumblers opposite. Nevertheless, an awareness of the fact that all is not well in the land has penetrated the consciousness across the aisle. Good. They have decided to do something about it; also good.
This is not the time to address its program per se. However, it really cannot be avoided entirely because, as I see it, the only reason the Bill before us now has been presented to the House is to support that forlorn, desperate six and five program. This Party supported that program, but we did so as a by no means ideal method of addressing the problem at issue, the malfunctioning economy, which had been brought to its present disastrous state by the policies of the Party in power, the Party that now wants the collusion of this House in making its makeshift repairs.
Secondly, we did so, as has already been made abundantly clear, with the intention of limiting its effects on the working population of this country. It is not the intention of my Party to ride out this depression or recession-Mr. Speaker, let us call a spade a spade-on the backs of the poor and it is certainly not our intention to do so on the backs of the elderly. Surely we have enough resources to hand in this blessed nation of ours that we need not set our so-called golden-agers adrift on an economic ice floe, an ice floe marked six and five.
Let me reiterate. The only justification for this unjust and unnecessary Bill is that it supports the program of six and five. Six and five has, in fact, become more than a program. It has become more than a slogan. It has sort of become a golden calf. "Bow down to the golden calf marked six and five, and if enough people do, we can be re-elected."
Like Kilroy of World War II fame, who scribbled his name on everything movable and immovable on the continent of Europe, this Government has to scrawl its "Kilroy was here"
November 25, 1982

on all within its ever-reaching grasp, only it is not "Kilroy was here," it is six and five.
What about public sector wages? They are under the six and five umbrella. I would point out to the Liberal Party on the other side and those to my left that when we voted for the original six and five we voted for restraint on our own salaries as well. Yes, the public goes for it. Then private sector firms with Government contracts sell six and five across the country. It has spread the word of six and five. Everything, you name it, is six and five, with one exception, and that exception is the Government's own spending and Government-administered prices. The Government does not need to conform to six and five. No, not the Liberals.
What about Old Age Security? It is six and five for Old Age Security, you want to believe it. What a cheap shot. What a low blow. The generation which now comprises our senior citizens, the generation to which I am proud to belong, is one which has paid its dues. Many of us have lived, struggled and survived through two wars and a depression. This is a record of survival to which this Government seems determined to add a second depression. These people have scraped and sacrificed to bring to maturity the generations who form the work force of today. They do not owe us anything. We owe them. This is a pretty measly way of paying the debt. It is not as though this measure would have a significant effect on the deficit, or on any other aspect of the Government's fiscal or monetary stance. If it did, I, as a representative of the affected generation, would be prepared by all means to accept it as a part of the over-all package. But it does not. The amount by which Government pay-outs are reduced by the changes to the old age pension, the child tax credit and the family allowance comes to about $10 million. That is peanuts. It is literally peanuts compared to the amounts blown, for example, on bailouts for corporate friends of the Party across the aisle, or perhaps it is a still grosser insult to our collective intelligence and integrity compared to the amount by which the public purse was looted to buy out the competition for our so-called "window on the oil industry."
It bespeaks a strange ordering of priorities that we see there across the aisle, and a strange, a very strange, ranking of values. I am aware that the Liberals propose to increase the Guaranteed Income Supplement by an amount sufficient to offset the reduction in basic Old Age Security in the hands of those who receive it, and for this gesture, at least, I commend them. But as a matter of principle, I favour simplicity, be it in legislation itself or in the administrative procedures which support that legislation.
Those of our elderly citizens who do not need Old Age Security and would be relatively unaffected by its not being fully indexed would return the difference in their income tax payable under the tax legislation already in force. In short, the measures we have before us here will serve only to complicate the administrative procedures already in place. In fact, this legislation serves no useful purpose whatsoever. It renders more complex an already complex procedure. It does not greatly affect the Government's fiscal or monetary stance. It
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
does one thing and one thing only. It provides one more surface upon which the Government can stretch six and five. That, effectively, is all that it does. As the sole reason for deindexing an entire generation, and this generation above all, it is reprehensible.
I want here to re-emphasize a point made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). Elderly, single pensioners with incomes of $9,000 will lose $290 in this two-year period. But a couple with two children and an income of $27,000 will lose less than $50 during the same time frame. Is this what the Government intends? As I see it, there can be only two reasons for this inequity. Either this is the Government's intention, this is the effect it really wants to create, or-and this conclusion would seem inescapable-it really has no idea what it is doing at all.
The Government wanted to appear to have a program. Above all, it wanted to have one more thing upon which to hang the slogan of six and five, and so, with no more consideration of its downstream effects than that, it has hatched the Bill that sits before us now. I do not want to believe this. I do not want to believe what the Lord knows. But on the basis of what we see before us and how this Government has operated in the past, I must conclude that this is very possible.
There is yet another matter which should be looked at, and that is the question of the demographics of our population. There is a hump which is passing along the demographic chart, a hump representing the post-World War II baby boom. This hump is at present well within the work force age group, but at some stage in the not too distant future that hump is going to pass into the category of senior citizen. Some time fairly soon the proportion of our population 65 years of age or over will radically increase. If we approach that time with the same set of assumptions in place as now exist, we are going to have a very serious set of problems on our hands. This is not news; we are all aware of it. But we have not yet done anything to anticipate the adjustments that will have to be made.
I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that this presents a most opportune time to do so. It is a time of crisis when the Government insists that certain changes must be made in the Old Age Security legislation. Perhaps it is the time when we should examine all the parameters of our Old Age Security system and decide just what we want of it, what we want it to do and how we want it to be structured to meet the conditions of the present day, 20 years from now and beyond, even into the twenty-first century. I want to suggest that this should be a time for thoughtful building and of far-reaching decisions well reasoned out.
The role that Old Age Security has played and has been expected to play in our society has changed and developed through the years. The legislation must be expected to face some dramatically altered conditions over the next several years. I suggest that if we are to tamper with it now, then that tampering should be done in order that it may better meet the

requirements we and the Canadian people shall demand of it in the years to come.
It is not the time to take a heedless measure such as this one before us now which hurts many, benefits no one, including the Government's deficit position, except in a very minor way, and is introduced for no reason except to further impress the stamp of six and five.

Health Minister Monique Begin suggests old-age pensioners should be at the forefront in the fight against inflation. Quite right. So many of them were at the front during two world wars and at least one depression-why should they be allowed to rest on their laurels?
It would seem that this is what the Minister and the Government wish to portray.

She was very proud when she received that pension because it was her own money. She was proud to take that money rather than accept money from her daughters, even though she took excellent care of the household.
Of course, pensions have risen dramatically since then. In those days one had to undergo a means test before receiving a pension. You had to prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that you had nothing. Today, the old age pension is a right to which all senior citizens are entitled. There is no stigma attached to it at all. The stigma attached to old age pensioners today is the fact that they are having to cut corners in their everyday lives because of inflation and the high cost of many goods and services today. Our old age pensioners are finding it difficult to get along.
The cost of clothing has been mentioned. I suppose we should be thankful that senior citizens do not have to buy as many new clothes as those who are in the work force or younger people. I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare is certainly very sympathetic. I see some of my hon. friends looking at me with surprise when I say that. i would like to put my comments on the record with regard to this legislation, Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. The purpose of this Bill is to limit the indexation of Old Age Security to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. In essence, this is an application of the Government's six and five policy to the pension system.
The six and five policy is the Government's so-called economic strategy. I say "so-called" because it really is a sham. Inflation has been decreasing in spite of the program. It is not surprising that inflation has been coming down, given the depth of the recession that we are in today and even the predictions made by the Conference Board of Canada that the recession will last longer than was foreseen. While inflation has been coming down, wages have been trailing inflation.
Why did the Government come up with the six and five program? It is my judgment that the Government has no economic policy but could not appear before the Canadian people to reveal that fact. It had to put up some sort of a front and the front was the six and five. It decided that it would "attack inflation". Then as inflation comes down due to the depth of the recession, it can claim credit for having done something about inflation and for having an effective economic policy. This is not economic policy; this is political strategy of the worst kind.
The other day The Globe and Mail quoted a study on wages by Citibank of New York and it demonstrated that wages in Canada have in fact been trailing those of most other western industrialized countries. The notion that the Government has been putting forward that somehow unjustified wage demands are the cause of our weakness in the international market today just does not stand up when examined and analysed, and it certainly was refuted by the Citibank study.
You have to ask, Mr. Speaker, if wages are not the cause of our problems in the international market, why has the Government focused its attention on wages, through six and five and the pension system? It is my conclusion that the Government simply wanted to put up a good front. It wants to be able to say to people that it is doing something, when in fact it is not. This is political strategy, not economic strategy.
1 want to turn to the application of the six and five principle to pensions specifically. The Government claims that it will be saving some $31 million by this measure. Some of the calculations that we have done have indicated that it will be taking even more than that from the pockets of pensioners. Clearly, it is not going to have any real impact on the deficit.

in the past many women were deprived of an adequate income because they stayed home to raise their children. That should be corrected. Mr. Speaker, normally I receive a great deal of pleasure in speaking to the various Bills which come into this House, but this afternoon I speak to Bill-131 with a certain degree of sadness and regret. Because in this Bill I see the destruction of what I think is a fairly good pension system for Canada.
Our pension system rests on four tiers. We have the Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which give

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
a basic amount of money to people who retire, we have the Canada Pension Plan which supplements that amount of money for those people in the working force, and we have private pension plans, which are many and varied. Finally, of course, we have personal savings, which include our house and mortgage and RRSPs. This system provides a fairly good pension system in this country.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) I am happy to see is in the House this afternoon, because it must take a great deal of courage to come in and support this Bill which I know in her heart of hearts she does not support. The Hon. Minister travelled throughout Europe and examined the pension systems there. On her return she said the two systems which provide the best Government support are in Sweden and in Canada. I agree with the Minister, but my question is, why then Bill C-131? This Bill portends the destruction of our basic pension system.
It is not often that I agree with the Hon. Members on the far left side of this House, but I do agree with the statement made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) that this Bill cancels out the universality of OAS. The Minister became very upset when the Hon. Member made that statement, but I can tell you why it is true. First of all, this Bill allows for indexing only to the extent of 6 per cent for OAS this year and 5 per cent next year. At the moment our inflation rate is well over 10 per cent. If it stays that way, gradually more importance will be placed on GIS and there will be fewer and fewer people relying on OAS. Eventually, we will have a system where most of the money for that basic pension system is under GIS. We will not have a universal system then because GIS is income-tested, and if most of those poor over 65 years of age are getting their basic money from GIS, how can we say we have a universal system?
I suggest that the Minister agrees with me, and 1 would like to quote from the National Pension Conference where she said:
Consider another key issue; pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years. People who thought they had purchased protection for the rest of their lives find they have more serious financial problems the older they become.
Of course. That is exactly what is going to happen. It should be recognized by the people of Canada that Bill C-131 marks the beginning of the end for our universality in the OAS system, which was at one time the pride of this country.
1 would like to quote from the Minister again, and if I am wrong, I hope she corrects me. On September 26, 1981, in an article in the Vernon Daily News which stated 54 per cent of pensioners receive GIS, the Minister said: "That's scandalous; there's something wrong in the system." I agree with the Minister. The Guaranteed Income Supplement was originally put into the system only to support those few people who did not quite reach the poverty level with the moneys they were getting from their retirement schemes. It is scandalous that instead of covering just a few people it now covers a great majority, and it will have to cover more people in the future because of this Bill which the Government has placed before this House. Certainly Bill C-131 represents, 1 think it is fair to
say, the kind of double-talk, double-thinking and double-cross which has gone on with this Government over the past two and a half years. Its action certainly does not follow its words.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at a national press conference said: "We are determined to bring about substantial pension reforms during our present mandate." Is Bill C-131 pension reform? It is taking money away from pensioners who are at or about the poverty line and bringing many more pensioners down close to it. Surely everyone knows what the poverty line is. It is an "Alice in Wonderland" figure, because if you happen to live in a city where expenses are high it is different than if you live in the country and own your own home.
This Bill is from a Government whose Minister of National Health and Welfare at the time the Government first brought in this particular Act, the Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh, stated on November 9, 1964 and I quote from Hansard at page 9899:
-that all future old age security pensions will be pegged to the cost of living index and will increase automatically if living costs increase.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Of course, the Hon. Members would say "Hear, hear". It was a good idea then and it is a better idea now because of high inflation. She went on to say, and I again quote from Hansard at page 9899 of that date:
This is a new departure in old age security. It is in response to the oft heard cry of those in receipt of pensions that they are unable to keep up with their own expenses if the cost of living rises-
These are the words of a Minister who paid attention to the "oft heard cry" of poor pensioners. I ask this Minister, what has she done in this respect? I am quite prepared to agree that pension payments are a very large problem in this country. They take a large part of our gross national product. Last year it totalled somewhere around $7.5 billion, which was 3 per cent of the gross national product. That has doubled since 1966 when old age pensions only took about 2 per cent of the gross national product. It is estimated that in 1990 old age pensions will take 12 per cent of the gross national product, and in the year 2025 will take 18 per cent of the gross national product. There is no doubt that it is an area that should concern this House and deserves a lot of time and study, because we can rest assured that in the future we are going to have great difficulty in this particular area.
That is why I find it so difficult to understand. Instead of building, as it promised to do, instead of helping pensioners, this Government continues to destroy them. It is not that the Government does not recognize the problems. The Canadian Government report on aging, a briefing book used by this Government, says that inflation has had a serious effect on the real value of pensions and annuities. There is an emerging consensus that corrective action must be taken.
Now, why, I ask you, when this is the kind of thing the Government puts out in books, do we have an Act like this which reduces the indexing of our basic pension scheme? The
November 25, 1982

OAS is the pedestal upon which everything is built. It is no answer to say, "Well, we are going to increase GIS so no one will fall below the poverty line." It is that group of people just above the poverty line who will lose money. They will not be affected by the GIS because they will not qualify, and we will be taking money from the poor. I think it is a national scandal that we should have that kind of legislation and expect the people of this country to sit idly by.
Earlier someone mentioned the demographic problem we are having. It is very true that from 1946 to 1966 there was a large increase in the number of births in Canada. I think the biggest result is, and everyone should be well aware of it, that at the moment there are seven workers supporting one pensioner. In the year 2025 when that population bulge reaches retirement age there will be two, or three at the most, workers supporting every pensioner.
So the question we have to ask ourselves now is, will those workers continue to pay the kind of taxes necessary to support those pensioners? We have already seen the experience of Sweden where there was a tax revolt among the workers. They refused to pay taxes because too much was being taken from them.
Not long ago I had the opportunity, along with some other Members of this House, to go to Vienna for a conference on aging. I would like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare for giving me that opportunity. My only regret is that she was not able to accompany us. At that conference some 1,200 people from some 100 countries talked about the same kind of problem we have here, the problem of an aging population with the number of aged growing dramatically in the next couple of decades. During the two weeks we spent there a great deal of work was done by the delegates preparing a plan of action which would later go to the United Nations, presumably to be adopted by the UN and then given to all countries. It was really a plan of action for guidance as to how to handle the problem of the aged and the aging in all societies. Canada is not alone in this, and many countries, even some Third World countries, will face far more serious problems than we in this regard.
In any event, they came to many conclusions, of course. One was that you cannot deal simply with the question of pensions; you have to deal with the whole problem of aging. You have to deal with health problems because the aged generally have more health problems, therefore requiring more government expenditures. You have to deal with housing for senior citizens. How do you involve senior citizens in this whole process? Because, as we all know, senior citizens are healthier and more active than they have ever been and want to get involved.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, that conference in Vienna came up with a plan of action, well over 100 recommendations. The Canadian Government was there, ably represented, and we did very well, I thought, in terms of making a great contribution. I presume the Canadian Government adopted and signed this plan of action; at least, that was its purpose. I would just like to read recommendation No. 28, Subsection (b), which says that we must ensure that the minimum benefits will be enough to meet the essential needs of the elderly and guarantee their
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
independence. Social security payments should be adjusted taking into account previous income. Efforts should be made to maintain their purchasing power. Ways should be explored to protect the savings of the elderly against the effects of inflation.
Here we have a Bill which this Government has put before us, Bill C-131, which reduces indexation for old age pensioners to well below the inflation rate. This is the Government which worked on and signed this document. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how can Liberal backbenchers sit there and not protest? Not one of them has spoken on this Bill. Not one. If they think so much of it, why do we not hear a few words as to why it is a good thing? Because they know it is not a good thing, they know it is a very bad thing. I do not think we can long survive if we do not pay more attention to the needs of our elderly.
It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, that the Government is imposing six and five on our pensioners, yet it never seems to go the other step and index its own expenditures and requirements. I would like to refer to a Supply and Services memo which I hold in my hand dated August, 1982. This memo indicates that pensioners at level one, with family coverage, face a 32.38 per cent increase in their premium rate for group surgical and medical insurance. Now, what kind of justice is that? The Government limits the pensioners to 6 per cent and then increases their costs 32 per cent. No wonder that no member of the Government is prepared to get up and talk on this particular Bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: They have been told to keep quiet.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That can be the only reason.
I remember, Mr. Speaker, the first Throne Speech that I heard. In that speech the Governor General said that the House of Commons will be asked to consider a program of action designed to respond to individual needs by promoting greater security for the elderly. Now, what has happened? Surely Bill C-131 does not promote greater income security for the elderly. Yet here we are two and a half years later fulfilling the program of this Government. If that is not double-talk and double-think and double-cross, I really do not know what is.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have heard a lot about Bill C-133 and the large amount of opposition coming from a few Government members. They are saying they will not vote for any Bill which limits to six and five the indexing of civil servants' retirement benefits. They say it is the breaking of a contract, and I agree with them. But it is kind of interesting that most of that talk is coming from Members in Ottawa who have large numbers of civil servants as constituents. There is nothing wrong with that, but have they forgotten all about the other elderly people who receive OAS? Where is some word of support from the backbenches of the Government for all those other elderly poor? It is very, very strange. One would almost think that they only vote this way when it is to their political advantage to do so. Why are they prepared to defend organized lobby groups but are not prepared to speak out on behalf

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
of the unorganized elderly? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that those Members who have said they will put their seat on the line for the superannuates should do the same thing for the hundreds of thousands of elderly poor who will be affected by this legislation.
Hon. Members opposite should realize that a lot of the people in their constituencies whose OAS will be reduced by six and five have sons and daughters. If we have an election within the next two years, I suspect that a lot of those elderly people and their sons and daughters and grandchildren will remember what is happening today when they go to vote. On average, this Bill will directly affect the pocketbooks of 13.5 per cent of eligible voters in the country, and in some ridings the percentage will be higher.
Until recently the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), who is not in the House, has been very vocal about the effect this legislation will have. I wonder if he realizes that 14.9 per cent of eligible voters in his riding receive OAS? I am sorry that the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) is not present today, because 17.7 per cent of his constituents receive OAS and they will be affected by this legislation. I am told that in the constituency of the Minister of National Health and Welfare only 8.2 per cent of constituents receive OAS. Perhaps the Prime Minister is not worried if he is not going to run again, but over 19 per cent of his constituents receive OAS and they will be affected by the legislation.
The Government should reconsider this legislation and the effect it will have upon the elderly. According to what it claims, its intentions are of the best. Certainly the Minister of National Health and Welfare has gone across the country talking about the problems of the pension system and about the 500,000 elderly men and women who live under the poverty line. She has promised that her first priority is to help them. I understand some of the difficulties she faces because the Government changes the Finance Minister almost as often as the Prime Minister changes the flower in his lapel. I suppose this makes it difficult for her to communicate.
For about two years we have heard about the green paper on pensions which the Government is going to bring forth. 1 plead with the Minister to expedite this. Speaker after speaker has said that we face a horrendous cost in the financing of pensions for the elderly in the years ahead. We know that if the Canada Pension Plan fund is not increased it will soon be without money, and that by the year 2001 there will be a net outgo. We also know that private pension plans have to be improved. There will need to be more coverage and earlier vesting.
The country is prepared to discuss these things, but that cannot take place until the Government offeis an over-all plan.
Experts hold that an average employer who contributes $100 today will have to contribute $350 in the future to pay for the improvements to private pension plans. Surely the country deserves the opportunity to discuss these things.
The Canadian Labour Congress has spoken about increasing the amount of the CPP contribution from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. That would impose a tremendous cost on both employer and employee, but it is something that should be discussed. There are people who favour an increase in the Canada Pension Plan generally to overcome some inequities, particularly those suffered by women. That is another matter that we should discuss. There are other alternatives. The public is entitled to enter the discussion and to be presented with the facts. I plead with the Minister to bring the green paper forward so that we can get on with improving the security of old age pensions, as the Government promised.
I am sure we all know that we live in what is called a "zero sum" society-that you do not get anything out unless someone else puts something in. We all know that our capacity and ability to provide social services, such as pensions and health care, depends on productivity. We all know as well-except perhaps some Members to my left who do not seem to understand it-that there is no such thing as a free lunch. With all this talk about improving pensions, we must also talk about improving productivity. The job cannot be done by Members of the Opposition, however; it has to be done by the Government. Why has the Government waited so long, Mr. Speaker?
This Party will fight tooth and nail against the legislation as it stands, because it is bad legislation. It affects virtually every senior citizen in the country.
Someone has said the measure will bring the Government $31 million. The Government has already spent $100 million on advertising and $25 million for a monument in darkest Africa. It is a shame that it does not look after the people of the country better.
Again, I plead with the Government to withdraw this legislation which will be a hardship on the elderly poor of the nation.
