November 25, 1982
All items preceding No. 54 allowed to stand by unanimous consent.

That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of any agreement signed between the Enterprise Development Board and General Aluminum Forging Ltd. of Hamilton, Ontario, including copies of all communications and minutes of meetings between the two parties prior to the signing of the agreement.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise with some measure of sadness this afternoon, recognizing that we are coming to the end of this Thursday afternoon "Hal Herbert Happy Hour". The changes in the rules which we hope will go into effect at the end of December will mean that this, 1 was going to say "ridiculous" but I guess I should not call it a ridiculous procedure, but a procedure which is rather ineffectual, will be terminated.
I must admit that I was a Member of the committee that made the recommendation to the House that has been accepted-and I fully support it-to change the rules to eliminate this procedure which we go through regularly on a Thursday afternoon. It is a procedure which has come about simply because the session has gone on so long that we find ourselves looking for something to fill up the hour between five o'clock and six o'clock on a Thursday.
In an attempt to pick a subject of interest I chose this motion, which incidentally goes back quite a way. In fact, it originated with a news release in December of 1980 when the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce announced:
-that the Enterprise Development Board has agreed to provide support to General Aluminum Forgings Ltd. of Winnipeg, Manitoba in the form of a guarantee of 90 per cent of $3.1 million loan to be raised by the company, a subsidiary to Sterlake Enterprises Ltd. of Hamilton, Ontario. The company is establishing a new facility at Winnipeg to manufacture precision aluminum forgings.
Total cost of the facility will be in the region of $7.1 million.
Construction of the new plant has already started and it is anticipated that the plant will be ready by the fall of 1981. The plant is expected to provide employment for about 52.
The release went on to say that the Minister and his officers:
-have been in touch with the McDonnell-Douglas Corporation which has offered to place contracts with the new firm as part of the industrial benefits accruing from the CF18 new fighter aircraft.
I know nothing of the company referred to in the news release. 1 do not want to say that I am not interested in the company; I am interested in any company which is operating in an efficient fashion, but the primary motivation of the motion is not the company itself. Immediately following the
Enterprise Development Board
release, I wrote to the Minister in December, 1980 in which I put this simple question to him:
-what does the Government receive, if anything, in return for its guarantee?
Being unaware of the way the system worked, I asked:
Is there any DREE money in this project?
My letter was dated December 11, 1980. As so often is the case-and I have spoken about this many times before-I waited patiently and nothing was forthcoming-no response, no acknowledgement. On April 3, 1981, I put a motion on the Order Paper, the one that is up for discussion today.
On May 6, 1981 I received a response to my letter of December, 1980. I want to read the relevant parts of it and I emphasize once again that this discussion does not centre particularly upon the company named in the motion but upon the procedures and support programs of the Government. In his letter the Minister said:
-EDP structures financial packages and insures loans for companies, particularly smaller and medium-sized operations, who encounter difficulties in obtaining financial backing because of the risk factors in relation to the size of the operation involved. All loan insurance is on a last resort basis, that is, when financing is not available on reasonable terms without the insurance.
In the particular case of General Aluminum Forgings Inc., it was the judgment of the Enterprise Development Board that a loan guarantee was necessary to enable the principals to secure the financing needed to establish the plant.
Then the Minister went on to say:
To answer your question, the Government itself does not materially receive anything in return for its guarantee, with the exception of a recoverable 1 per cent insurance fee, but rather achieves some success for the event which, in turn, contributes to job creation and industrial development. In this particular case, the loan guarantee contributed directly to the creation of 52 jobs-
The Minister also told me in his letter:
DREE will also participate in the project and has made a grant offer of $1,265 million based on estimated eligible capital costs of $4.02 million. Both the EDP loan insurance and the DREE grant are contingent upon a company contribution or investment of $1.5 million.
Those are the details. What I was looking for was, of course, the general Government approach to assistance to industry. As I said, the motion was placed on the Order Paper in April, 1981. With nothing forthcoming in the way of documents, the motion was transferred for debate on December 16, 1981. Even after a motion is transferred for debate-in other words, the motion for the production of papers is no longer there for the Government to act upon-there is no reason the Government should not produce documents at that particular point in time. Alternatively, it might contact the Member-and whether it is a Government Member or an Opposition Member is irrelevant-and discuss the information which the Member is seeking. Surely the purpose is to ensure that Members are as well informed as possible.
In my own case my interest was not in the company named in the motion but in the operation of the program. Obviously because I represent an area with a large industrial base, I was interested in ensuring that the companies in my own riding would have full knowledge of the program and would be able to take advantage of any of its benefits.
20990

November 25, 1982
Enterprise Development Board
I should put on the record the little I learned about the Enterprise Development Program. Apparently it was introduced in April of 1977 by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It was to replace the Automotive Adjustment Assistance Program, the Program for Advancement of Industrial Technology, the General Adjustment Assistance Program, the Pharmaceutical Industry Development Assistance Program, the Industrial Design Assistance Program, the Program to Enhance Productivity, and the Footwear and Tanning Industry Adjustment Program. Those fancy-sounding names are all represented by initials. I am now led to believe that two of them, PAIT and IDAP, no longer exist. Also it was introduced because:
Responding to messages from Canadian businessmen to make programs more widely know and more easily understood, IT and C formulated EDP to subsume these programs. The forms of support that were available under the old programs are available under EDP.
I was trying to make the Program more widely known in my own riding and for the benefit of all businessmen. If documents are lodged on the floor of the House, then they are in the public domain and available to everyone. The forms of assistance under the Program were loans or loan insurance for adjustment projects, grants for innovation projects, grants for product design, grants to study productivity improvement projects, grants to identify new products, and so on. These were all very well described.
I should like to refer to a private publication, a publication of Price, Waterhouse entitled "Government Financial Assistance Programs in Canada," which indicated under the heading "Objective":
The program is designed to provide financial support, by means of grants and/or loan assistance, to Canadian businesses involved in high risk and innovative projects or adjustment projects designed to increase efficiency and competitiveness-
Surely today we need to increase efficiency and competitiveness. I continue:
-that can be expected to yield attractive rates of return on the total investment and/or provide economic benefit to Canada through an increase in, or sustaining of, exports and/or employment.
What could be more worthy?
Before coming into the House I wanted to refer to the latest annual report of the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In my files I have the 1980-1981 report. I asked for the 1981-1982 report, which would be for the year ending March 31, 1982. I am sorry to report that the 1981-1982 annual report of the Department has failed to be produced. I am sorry because, of course, I can only then look at what was happening a couple of years ago as shown in the 1980-1981 report. I read in the report of that year the following:
The Enterprise Development Program (EDP) provides assistance to manufacturing and processing firms to improve their viability and international competitiveness.
During 1980-1981, 151 adjustment assistance loan guarantees valued at $231 million were authorized. In addition, $98.2 million in contributions were authorized towards the cost of 549 innovation and product development projects
in such industries as machinery electronics, chemicals, ship components, automotive vehicles, building components and textiles.
Under the program, insurance of $111.5 million was authorized for 142 loans made by private lenders to manufacturing firms.
I had a secondary interest in pursuing this particular motion on this subject. Ever since I came here I have taken an interest in the Estimates which are tabled every year. I have studied them. It took me many years before I had any idea of how I could either read these Estimates or make any sense out of them. I must admit I am still much confused, even after being here ten years. I find it sometimes very difficult to obtain answers that I would accept as satisfactory.
My question to the Minister contained in the motion obviously deals with any benefits occurring to the Government to compensate it for its risks. I was told about the 1 per cent, which is the insurance charge.
In the Estimates for 1981-1982, one can read under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce that the insurance payments under the Enterprise Development Program show expenditures for 1979-1980 at zero. One can read that the Estimates for 1980-1981 are also indicated as zero. The Estimates for 1981-1982 are listed as $6.2 million. In that same book of Estimates one can also read under the heading "Industry Development":
Contributions to promote the establishment, improvement, growth, efficiency or international competitiveness of manufacturing, processing and service industries in Canada, including contributions under the Enterprise Development Program.
The forecast expenditures for 1980-1981 are shown as $60,673 million. The Estimates for 1981-1982 are shown as $76,638 million. I read these figures to show how one can be confused, because I then turned to the Estimates for 19821983. Under the same item for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the heading "Trade-Industrial Program" we see:
Statutory-Insurance Payments under the Enterprise Development Program.
We find that the expenditures for 1980-1981 are $8,402 million. Remember, I just read the Estimates for the previous year and they were zero. The Estimates for 1982-1983, the year in which we are at present, are $7.2 million. That is the expense that is shown in the Estimates for the Department.
Reading also from the 1982-1983 Estimates, in the same line as I read previously for 1981-1982, under the heading "Industry Development", I now see forecast expenditures for 1981-1982 of $142 million. Remember I read the Estimates for 1981-1982 and they were $76 million. From Estimates of $76 million, the figure has climbed to forecast expenditures of $142 million. The Estimates on that same page for the current year are shown as something over $124 million.
Thus, there are two motivations in bringing this particular motion to the House. I repeat, I do so not in any way to make any difficulties for the company concerned or to inquire into the business of the company that is mentioned in the motion. This motion is to inquire about the way the program operates. It is an attempt to publicize the work that is being done by the
November 25, 1982

Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in the industrial sector. It is also to inquire into the funds that are being used, the risks, the amount involved, the money we may lose as a result of our guarantees and the amount that comes back into the treasury, presumably into general revenues, since I cannot find this item in the Estimates.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, there are a multitude of questions on my mind even after all these years. I plead once again, because it appears we will not have this opportunity to discuss the subject much longer, that the Government try to help Hon. Members who are, in turn, trying to help the Government in being just a little freer in the way it provides information to us, to try to answer our questions and to try to provide us with the ammunition we need in order to sell Government programs.
As I said at the beginning, we may be near the end of this particular period on a Thursday afternoon when we can discuss motions for the production of papers. I wonder if anything has been accomplished over the years of trying to change the system. I can only hope in the new year when the new rules of the House take effect and the new procedures are put into place that we will more effectively be able to encourage the Government to improve communications between Government Departments and Members of Parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for his presentation on his motion. I believe that, like all motions, it is significant, and the right answers and the right solutions must be found if issues raised by Hon. Members are to be given satisfactory clarification. There is a problem, however, and that is how to answer all questions simultaneously, and how to be very specific in a case where there is still a confidential aspect to be reckoned with.
Therefore, I understand the Member for Vaudreuil who has been waiting for a long time to get information on this company, namely, General Aluminum Forging Ltd. This case was of particular interest to Manitoba, because of the company's job creation potential, which is directly related to the aerospace industry. To get to the subject of the motion itself, I would like to explain to the Hon. Member that when the plant was opened on October 30, 1981, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) gave all the facts on the kind of subsidies, the exact amounts of those subsidies and what programs had been used to give direct assistance to the company in establishing its facilities.
But before going any further, I would like to explain for the benefit of the House, that at the Department of Industry and Commerce, we have one basic tenet, and that is the confidentiality of certain documents. Failure to observe this rule would jeopardize the industrial strategies of certain companies vis-avis their competitors, and therefore, when examining a particular case, it would be unthinkable to publish all elements of our
Enterprise Development Board
negotiations with the company, because then we would get to the point where we would no longer be able to guarantee confidentiality to a company that has put its trust in the department. The department must ensure that its programs are known to the public and clear in their objectives concerning demand, but it must also protect the confidentiality of the details of each case, and just as we at the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE deal with the confidentiality of corporate files, the Department of National Revenue, for instance, is responsible for the confidentiality of the files of individuals.
Therefore, when an Hon. Member demands production of papers before an agreement is signed, there are many factors, including the legislation and regulations in effect and the rule of confidentiality, that prevent the minister from producing papers at that time. Similarly, once the agreement has been finalized, and once the actual work has begun, certain aspects of the file cannot be published without jeopardizing a company's competitive position, since free competition is one of the principles of our economic system.
That being said, for the benefit of the Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) I should now like to provide the following information regarding the agreement with General Aluminum Foreign Ltd. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce contributed $1.5 million to the project, while the Federal Development Bank provided a minimum loan of $700,000. That was the Federal Government's contribution under the program, and if the Member for Vaudreuil wants to know more about the various programs, perhaps I could tell him about the funds available at the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the funds allocated to each program, and the percentage earmarked for Quebec, Ontario and Canada as a whole. Of course, I would have liked the department to get me the necessary information more quickly so that I could give the Hon. Member a more complete answer. I believe that it is important to give a direct answer, because, as too often happens in the House of Commons, Hon. Members indulge in lengthy debates just for the purpose of killing time, and I deplore this, and personally, I would have preferred to have a more thorough discussion of the legislation this afternoon. I agree with my Hon. colleague who asked that the rules be changed. I think this is vital because, Mr. Speaker, what this country needs is hard work. There is urgent legislation before the House, and if we start providing information like this at the end of the day just for the sake of making the 5 to 6 period a little more interesting, I think the rules of the game should be changed very quickly, for the benefit of all concerned.
Now, to provide some clarification of the budget of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I may point out that for the year 1980-81, $98.2 million were set aside for subsidies under the Enterprise Development Program, and of

November 25, 1982
Enterprise Development Board
this amount, Quebec received more than $47.9 million or 48.8 per cent of the total budget for Canada. This was for subsidies, which are non-refundable. As for guaranteed loans, $231 million was budgeted for all of Canada, and of that amount, $25.5 million, or 11 per cent, was allocated to Quebec.
The purpose of the Enterprise Development Program is to enable companies in a strongly competitive market to become more diversified, more mechanized, and to introduce advanced technology in order to achieve strong penetration of new markets. This is vitally important. The department has a number of brochures that explain very clearly the exact objectives of the program and the types of subsidies available. I am not going to read them in the House, because I do not want to bore Hon. Members, but there are a number of programs of this kind that are available and that can be looked into at any time. Any suggestions for improvements will certainly be welcome and should be addressed to the minister or to departmental officials.
I referred earlier to the Enterprise Development Program and the grants and guaranteed loans for the defence industry. We often hear about this program and, in the case of the company mentioned in the motion, General Aluminum Forging Ltd., about how it relates to the defence industry. We often hear about these budgets in Quebec and Ontario. For the information of the Hon. Members, the total budget for the defence industry in Canada was $142.9 million in 1980-81, and Quebec received $66.6 million of this amount, or 46.6 per cent. This is enormous because the budget of the defence industry includes all technical research in the field of radar, radio and aerospace technology, which makes Quebec as well as Ontario more competitive with similar American industries. The same holds true for small business loans. The total budget in Canada is $408.4 million and Quebec received $120.9 million or 29.6 per cent of this total.
Another important matter, and the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) referred to it in his motion, is the budget of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. This matter is often discussed across Canada because people wonder what is really the mandate of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce compared with other Departments. I want to point out that the total budget of DREE for 1980-81 was $180.6 million, which amount was increased to $206.9 million in 1981-82. I believe that a good question to ask in this House would be: What is Quebec's share of this budget? Out of a budget of $180.6 million in 1980-81, Quebec received $118.4 million or 65.6 per cent, and out of a total budget of 206.9 million in 1981-82, $123.1 million was spent in Quebec, or 59.5 per cent. These figures speak for themselves and show how the presence of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE is important for a region.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is readily realized how important this can be for Eastern Canada, and so that the Chair may have all the relevant information, I have with me figures
for both Eastern and Western Canada. As concerns programs which benefit Eastern Canada, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce spends over 20 per cent of its total budget in the Atlantic provinces, which means that it considers regional economic development a major concern.
As for the motion of the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil, who has asked that certain documents be tabled, I would point out that the figures I have just mentioned are available to the public. They can be looked up at any time. As for the internal communications between the company involved and the Department, I would like to say that correspondence was exchanged over a period of two years and that there were also discussions meetings and minutes. In his motion, the Hon. Member requests that these minutes be made public, and this, at the request of the Department and the company before the negotiations. The parties involved agree on which documents will be made public and which will not be, and this is extremely important from a the procedural viewpoint. The Hon. Member has asked that the Department be allowed to provide more explanations, regardless of the rules, but it must be kept in mind that there will always be some documents which cannot be made public, and this holds true for any negotiation since certain interested parties must be protected. I therefore must say that, whatever amendments are made to the regulations, whether in the House or in the Department, there will still remain confidential elements in the Files.
Now that the file has been closed since the plant has been built, the situation has improved and the construction is now finalized, could other documents be made public? On this point, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil which specific documents he would like to see and which other maybe less important documents he would like to check.
At this stage, I would like to receive a formal request to go and check with the department, so that a distinction may be drawn between available and unavailable documents. To make the task of the Hon. Member easier it might also be useful at that point to ask the company itself whether or not it objects to our releasing certain documents because this is the third time I have to approach the department on that type of a case. The applicant company is always asked whether it agrees to the release of certain documents. This is most important, and neither party acts without the other's consent. Otherwise, documents of course could be leaked, and an application could be jeopardized for the sole reason that certain documents were to be kept secret at the negotiation stage.
Other aspects of the program are significant to industry and commerce, namely the Federal Business Development Bank. In respect of the program that was implemented concerning General Aluminum Forging Limited, I would like to point out that the Federal Business Development Bank made a concrete contribution within the business establishment itself. The
November 25, 1982

Federal Business Development Bank granted a $700,000 privileged loan on top of the $1.5 million put up by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Federal Business Development Bank loans across Canada totalled $484 million in 1980-81. That was the funding. There were $113.2 million for Quebec, or 23.4 per cent, and last year, for 1981-82, $460 million were available for loans, of which $163.9 million or 35.6 per cent for Quebec, which is enormous.
Concerning the Federal Business Development Bank, there is an interesting question that is often put in our areas: "Does the Federal Business Development Bank take risks? Do they have risk capital?" On that point I would like to state that $13.6 million are earmarked as risk capital for the whole of Canada, of which Quebec received $4.3 million, or 31.6 per cent of the 1980-81 funding. Also in 1981-82, there were $15.6 million available as risk capital for the whole of Canada, of which $4.7 million for Quebec, or 30.1 per cent of total loans granted in terms of risk capital. This is important, because it is often stated that the Federal Development Business Bank lends money at rates somewhat similar to those charged by chartered banks. But again caution is warranted here, because the Federal Business Development Bank does not give a loan unless the applicant was turned down by a chartered bank, and second, the Federal Business Development Bank rate is indeed lower than the market's. However, the main point here is that a significant amount of risk capital is available at the Federal Business Development Bank, which opens the way for closely monitored ventures.

In my view, the motion put by the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (M. Herbert) boils down to a request for information in the first place: First on the company as such, the negotiations that were held between the department and the company. So 1 will carry on on this subject, because I have information here from my office that can be of use to every Member in this House. Well, as far as the small business development bond is concerned, this is very interesting, and I read: $3,553 billion for Canada last year, that is for fiscal 1980-81. Perhaps I might digress briefly and mention that it was thanks to the Corporation that Bombardier was able to gain a
Enterprise Development Board
foothold on the American market, to the same extent that we were able with Aerospace to export Canadian technology as far away as Brazil. That is very important because, when the provinces make certain claims on the federal government, the officials in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion may just be somewhat slow on the uptake in the sense that they fail to provide information in terms which people may readily understand. But when we are dealing with figures ranging between $3.5 billion and $4.5 billion, I think we ought to be specific. However, now that the department has been restructured, we do have some reservations.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I have heard hon. colleagues expressing some concern about the restructuring of DREE. It is practically common knowledge that what we now have is pitched battle between senior officials of the department, who are wondering who is going to get which position. Functions are being centralized, while the original purpose of the department was, of course, to develop the regions. They are centralizing in the large urban centres, comfortably ensconced in their ivory towers, and the bureaucracy-I am sure my hon. colleagues opposite are going to appreciate this, since they are very unhappy about all the bureaucracy in Government-the bureaucracy is steadily increasing and we now have a department that is practically immune to change. I forget which French writer said that bureaucracy was a monster administered by pygmies. That is quite true, when you think about it.

For instance, DREE in Montreal has 190 employees, in a department which is supposed to be concerned with regional economic development. Montreal has 190, Quebec City has 40, and in the regions where the work is actually done, there are 20. That gives a pretty clear picture of how this bureaucracy operates. It is more or less the same in the other provinces. So there certainly is cause for concern. And what kind of results can we expect? Of course, since the department was restructured, it is now being led by an exceptional man who deserves all praise, but I wonder how one man is going to control this bureaucracy.
1 have the impression that my hon. colleague opposite has something to add, so if he is prepared to do so now, I am prepared to give him the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I thought 1 would get my colleague off the hotseat and maybe contribute a little. I know that he was struggling very hard to keep the debate going. I do have a contribution to make. In Notice of Motion No. 54, the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) requests "a copy of any agreement signed between the Enterprise Development Board and General Aluminum Forging Ltd."
I have had a similar experience as the Hon. Member. I requested copies of the agreement between Imperial Oil and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources with regard to the loan to Imperial Oil to continue its activity in Cold Lake. It was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $40 million. We understand that part of the agreement, as indicated in the news release, was that if the plant did not go ahead within the year, the grant would be lost.
I think this is pertinent and follows very closely what we are talking about in this private members' hour. It is incumbent on the Government to make this agreement available so that we can fulfil our responsibility to our constituents and account for what the Government is doing. To do this, we must have access to these documents. I have repeatedly risen in this House under Standing Order 43, I have placed a motion on the Order Paper, I have questioned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), and the former minister of energy, mines and resources, with regard to the agreement which was signed at a cost of $40 million to the taxpayers of this country, and I have yet to receive the courtesy of a reply and I have yet to receive those documents. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, they will probably never see the light of day during this session of Parliament.
In the same vein, I have made repeated requests of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, again by way of the Order Paper, by questions in this House of Commons during Question Period, and by way of motions under Standing Order 43, for all relevant material, all studies done, which indicate what the impact on the economy of Canada would be with the construction of the Alsands project and the Imperial Oil project in Cold Lake. We are looking at a $12 billion to
Enterprise Development Board
$14 billion investment in the Alsands project and we are looking at a comparable investment in the Cold Lake project. Those are direct expenditure dollars, 1980 dollars. The direct flow-through, then, to the rest of the economy into virtually every Province in this country, the employment that it would generate, is vital information for this House of Commons I am convinced that if we had the available information which I requested with regard to those two plants all Members in this House would take a serious look at the policies which are forcing those two plants into oblivion. I am confident that these studies are in the hands of the departmental officials in Energy, Mines and Resources. I am also confident that if Hon. Members had access to that information, they would see the multiplication of the $24 billion investment in those two plants, what it would do to the economy over a 20 to 25-year period, and the jobs which could be created when we are in a position of having one and a half million people unemployed across the country.
When we see industries in Ontario and Quebec closing down, when we see whole communities shut down because they are dependent on a mine and the mine is closing out and when we see the auto industry pulling back, we can imagine the effect of a $24 billion investment in the oil sands which can produce energy security for Canada, which can create jobs across the country and inject into our economy an estimated $500 billion in a ripple effect. I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that if Hon. Members had access to the information which is there in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, probably sitting on a shelf, or maybe hidden on a shelf, I am sure there would be a revolt in the Liberal ranks, among backbenchers over there, that would make this Government's head spin.
It is the responsibility of all Members of this House, not only to play partisan politics, but to gather all the information which they possibly can in order to make sound decisions for the health of our country. I have just given two examples of information, such as agreements and studies, that should be available to all Members of this House yet are being held back.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil when he asks why this is not made available. I truly cannot see one reason why I should not have access or, indeed, any Member of this House, to the agreement which cost the Canadian taxpayers $40 million. I believe it is our right, Mr. Speaker, to have that agreement in our hands in order to ensure that the Government has used that money wisely. But all I was able to get was smart-aleck answers from the former minister of energy, mines and resources when I questioned him on that agreement.
I think it is the absolute right of every Member of this House of Commons to have in their possession copies of the studies done by Energy, Mines and Resources showing the impact on the economy right across the country with regard to the Alsands and the Cold Lake projects, because then, and only then, can we in this House do the job which we were sent here to do by our electors.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-131. I am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to follow my colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer). Of course, he is the pension critic for our party and
he knows a good deal about it, which will make it a little difficult for me to follow him. He knows so much about pensions for two reasons. First, obviously he has put an awful lot of work into his critic's role. Second, he has been collecting an old age pension himself for about 30 years. Well, I exaggerate a little.
I really want to talk about two things tonight with respect to what I think the Government is doing to our senior citizens. The Government is making things very hard for those people right now. Secondly, it is making sure that our senior citizens are going to have difficulties in the future. Essentially, what Bill C-131 sets out to do is to impose the famous six and five regime on a group which I believe is less able to bear that kind of hardship. I think all of us-certainly I do-approve of limiting Government spending, but not in this particular area. Why does the Government not look at eliminating some useless projects, some of these expensive things that we have watched the Government get involved in over the last year? But why, why, cut back on needed programs such as Old Age Security? The bulk of our senior citizen population in Canada depends very much on these pensions. They are not a cushion or extra income. They are in fact, in many cases, the only source of income. Of Canadians presently receiving Old Age Security, as I understand it, approximately one half or about 1.2 million Canadians, do not receive the guaranteed income supplement, but that does not mean they do not need it or could not use it. Many of those people are the ones who are going to feel the full impact of Bill C-131. They are the ones to be penalized by the Government, the very ones who have worked hard, planned and done everything possible to secure their financial independence for their old age. This Bill will jeopardize that security, jeopardize the savings they have worked for years and years to accumulate. It is also going to jeopardize, in many cases, something which is very important to these people, their own homes; the one thing that gives them a stable base and a real sense of security.
Indexing Old Age Security was the Government's answer to inflation. But not now. Now we find that the Government is going to place an unequal burden on a part of society which has virtually no clout with which to fight back. What the Government should be looking at is some kind of catch-up, not a penalty, which is certainly what Bill C-131 is all about. 1 do not think the Government has recognized the kind of limits there are on the savings of these people. The Government-I am sure this is going to happen-is going to force elderly Canadians to dig into their savings. That will have a particular impact today for one reason, the fact that people can now expect a much longer lifespan. They can expect to be pensionable for a much longer period of time. And what is very significant is that any losses they experience now are losses which will never be recouped. But the elderly are going to have to shoulder a permanent reduction in their standard of living because of what the Government calls, in Bill C-131, a temporary measure.
November 25, 1982

Let us stop and just look for a minute. Mr. Speaker, at private pensions. For example, they are not indexed. We also find that only about 40 per cent of our senior population enjoy private pensions. Therefore, many of our seniors will in fact lose their one inflation cushion, the one thing which allows them to cope with today's inflation. But it is not just a reduction of the savings of pensioners which is the problem. By keeping the amount that they receive at a lower level over the next two years, the Government is effectively reducing the base amount when full indexing returns. So the over-all pie is shrinking. Very simply, what that means is a permanent loss of that cushion against inflation. It is a permanent betrayal of this Government's promise. Senior citizens affected by Bill C-131 will live with six and five for the rest of their lives. It is going to become a permanent structure and permanent problem for them for as long as they live, and the Government insists on calling it a temporary measure.
If you look into the area of pensions in some detail, Mr. Speaker, you will find that it very much affects single people, and certainly women. We find that under the GIS the cut-off point for a single individual is around $8,900, and for couples it is about $15,000. That hovers very close to the poverty line. Anyone making that amount of money or more is fully indexed. Therefore, they will feel the full impact of Bill C-131. I think all of us would recognize that in this time of a high cost of living, $8,900 is not really very much. For a couple to live on $15,000, certainly in some of our urban areas, is not very much at all. In fact, it will be very difficult to maintain any kind of comfortable lifestyle on that income. Yet this Government has somehow managed to decide that it is enough to shoulder a part of what is supposed to be a temporary burden in the six and five fight. In fact, I think it is enough to threaten the savings of our senior citizens, and it is enough to limit their Old Age Security income forever.
We were relieved of course that the Government decided to use the GIS, but where we have some concern now is that many in fact will fall through that line which governs whether or not they will receive the GIS. As I mentioned earlier, that line is very close to the StatsCan poverty line.
I really believe that the Government has done the barest minimum it can to improve Guaranteed Income Supplement levels. It has been recommended that the GIS be used to bring even those who fall below that line, up to the level of the poverty line. This was recommended by the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association, the Canadian organization of small business and something called the Business Committee on Pension Policy. On April 20 the Minister indicated that she would be interested in doing that "as soon as funds are available", but it has never been done, Mr. Speaker. Instead, we find that there has been an attack on the whole plan of Old Age Security.
As I understand it, there are approximately 400,000 people in Canada receiving pensions-most of them women-who fall below the poverty line. The implications of this Bill for our
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
future is very important, Mr. Speaker. Earlier the Hon. Member for Okanagan North drew our attention to the effects of the baby boom, showing that at present there are seven workers for every pensioner and that by the year 2020 there will be three workers for every pensioner.
What I find frightening about the Government's approach to Bill C-131 is that it offers no comprehensive fiscal plan to deal with the problems that face us. The Canada Pension Plan will need contributions of around 9 per cent of earnings in future, instead of the present 3.6 per cent, to maintain the present level of benefit.
Unless some comprehensive planing takes place very soon, a heavy tax increase will have to be imposed on workers by the year 2000.
At the present time the Canada Pension Plan is short of cash. Things are very tight indeed. It tooks as if the fund will be bankrupt by the year 2020. A lot of the money in the fund has been lent to the Provinces at low rates of interest, and there is a popular belief that much of that money will never be paid back. It is imperative that Canadians, individually, be allowed to prepare for retirement independence. Instead of that, however, we find that the Government is aggravating the situation, and that will have an effect on the future. It is discouraging Canadians from investing for their old age or retirement. Interest borrowed on money to purchase RRSPs and Registered Home Ownership Plans is no longer tax deductible. This is another disincentive to deferred spending and to the intense saving that is usual in the years before a person buys a home. The RRSP was designed to give our senior citizens some measure of liquidity in their retirement years. The home is usually the single largest family asset that families can acquire, but this dream is becoming something of a pipedream now. It is the one thing that could have provided an accumulation of sale capital or accommodation security.
The foregoing are not only indirect barriers to savings, Mr. Speaker, there are others, such as the high level of taxation, the erratic interest rates that are eating up the savings of senior citizens and, worst of all, the economic mess the Government has created. It seems to be blindly forging ahead without trying to improve the situation. That is just a small list of the things that have been happening.
The unemployed are spending the reserves that they should have been able to put away for their retirement. The unemployed cannot save, they cannot buy homes, they cannot contribute to the Canada Pension Plan and they cannot contribute to their own private pension plans. The Government is creating a generation of pensions that will likely need full Government support just to stay at the poverty line. Private savings should be encouraged.
The Government should be worrying about the present state of the economy and looking to things like the National Energy Program to stimulate the economy and create jobs. It should be looking at ways to encourage deferred spending or, in other words, various forms of saving.

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The Government should be concentrating on preparing the country for the years ahead. It must look after its present obligations, but not by the means proposed in Bill C-131. The impact this Bill will have cannot be stressed enough. It will cut into the spending or the "coping power" of the senior citizens very severely. It will mean great hardship for them and will reduce the savings of those who have planned their retirement.
It seems that some Members of the Government have some reservations about reducing some pensions. A number of Members opposite have stated for the record that they will not support Bill C-133 in its present form. This Party will not support Bill C-133 nor will it support Bill C-131, Mr. Speaker.
Members of the Government seem to be able to make a distinction between the two classes of people affected by these Bills. On the one hand they are willing to protect the indexing that affects their own constituents, but they are not willing to do the same for the average senior citizen. Why are we not hearing from Members of the Government? Why are they not speaking out on this issue? Why have they decided not to support Bill C-133 but are prepared to go blindly ahead with Bill C-131?
Members of the Government who represented the capital region seem to understand why one Bill should not be meddled with but they cannot understand why the other should not. I do not think the other Members of the Government understand the implications of this. If they did, they would find themselves in a compromising position.
Bill C-131 would not have an equitable impact, Mr. Speaker. It would attack those least able to absorb the six and five regime, the group least able to influence changes on their own behalf. That group is being asked to shoulder a burden that will have a greater impact on them than on many other, if not all other, segments of Canadian society. It is not a temporary burden and it is not evenly distributed. It is a great contrast to the Government waste that we have seen over the last few years. It is a reduction in a program that is already underutilized, a program that needs growth, not pruning.
The Government does not recognize its responsibilities. It has shown a complete lack of willingness to look to the future and the problems it will bring. It is a Government that seems almost two-faced about its moral responsibilities and the narrow political motivations of its regional caucus.
I am pleased to have had this opportunity to speak on Bill C-131, Mr. Speaker. I think the Government should reconsider its stand on this legislation in direct correlation to Bill C-133.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate so far has been very constructive. I should like to commend my colleagues and all Members of the House who have taken part in it.
I contend that if the Members of the Party sitting on Mr. Speaker's right had really thought this Bill through, if they had put it in a realistic context, and if they had respect for the people it will affect, they would withdraw it. It is a bad Bill, and I will tell the House why. Like the rest of the six and five
program, it assumes its effect will be equal on all people if it is applied evenly to everyone.
I cannot understand how anyone can accept this line of thought. It must be obvious that a pensioner with a $20,000 per year income from stock dividends, maturing bonds, RRSPs or a private source can afford to lose a bit of real purchasing power, far more easily than a widow living on just over $8,900 per year, the cut off line for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
To put this income in context, Statistics Canada indicates that the poverty line for single individuals living in metropolitan areas is $8,922 or $10 more than the cut-off point for the Guaranteed Income Supplement. While it may be true that the GIS will be indexed to compensate for the limited indexation of the Old Age Security pension, the loss of any amount at all will be very difficult for the single pensioner whose income is about $9,000 to $10,000 per year, or the married couple with a combined income of slightly over $15,000 per year.
I would ask all Hon. Members to consider the restrictions and privations imposed by incomes this low. Assuming an inflation rate of only 7 per cent, a single pensioner will lose $150 over the next two years, while a couple, both over 65, will sacrifice $300. At 10 per cent inflation, the individual gives up $270 and the couple, $540. The low-income pensioner living on the edge of poverty just cannot afford this loss of buying power. That is one reason this is an unfair, mean-spirited Bill. It takes the greatest toll on those who can afford it the least.
Another reason I cannot support the Bill is that it penalizes the people who survived the hungry thirties, served their country in wartime and built up our industries in the post-war era. Assuming that 1.2 million pensioners will not qualify for the GIS, and that inflation will average 10 per cent, the Government will save $32.4 million from Old Age Security pensions over the next two fiscal years. The Government should not be proud of this. I do not believe our pensioners should lose almost $32.5 million of income, even in a period of restraint. I do not believe they should lose one penny.
Until the pension system is completely reformed, I contend that pensioners should not have desperate measures like the six and five grafted onto their income security program for the sake of blind uniformity. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said last Thursday night:
We are asking 1.1 million old age pensioners to help lead the way in the fight against inflation.
I say that her use of the word "ask" is a jarring euphemism.
I suggest that she actually ask a couple of hundred randomly-selected senior citizens if they support limited indexing of the Old Age Security pension, which is the only source of income for over 300,000 seniors in Canada. I coax her to ask them if they would volunteer to be on the front line of restraint. I am sure she would get quite a different tally of votes than the one the Government expects from the House.
Although $32.5 million is a lot of money, it pales in comparison with the $400 million the Government just spent to
November 25, 1982

strengthen the equity base of Canadair and de Havilland. It pales in comparison with the $500 million it is offering Dome Petroleum to help pull that Corporation out of its financial quagmire. I do not believe that many Canadians would disagree with maintaining the buying power of the old age pension for senior citizens, but any Member who listens to his or her constituents knows that many voters do not approve of big corporate bail-outs like the Dome deal.
The Minister of National Elealth and Welfare said that it would take roughly $250 million above current expenditures to bring 725,000 single and widowed Old Age Security pension recipients just up to the poverty line, but claimed that it was impossible to find the money elsewhere in any foreseeable future. Yet, she is a frontbencher of a Government that feels it is able to whisk away some $660 million from energy programs, $245 million from Official Development Assistance, and $230 million for national defence over the next two years for other programs.
On one hand the Government proposes to take radical measures to reduce inflation. On the other hand it has seen fit to add $400 million to the equity of de Elavilland and Canadair and to offer Dome $500 million, a sum which it may yet get to keep. Then there is the $990 million reduction in interest payments on the public debt. I am sure we would love to know what will become of that money. It certainly has not stopped the increase in unemployment. In the midst of all this free-floating capital, how can the Government hope to justify this mean, penny-pinching Bill? Obviously the Government does not have control of the purse strings. These anomalies are evidence of crisis management, piecemeal programming and a sad lack of a global overview of fiscal policy.
In short, the Government apparently has no idea how to save or spend public funds. Yet it touts six and five as if it were the cure for all ills, like a quack doctor's bloodletting, love potions and mustard plasters. The fiscal charlatanism the Government practises has not worked in the 12 years or so that it has held power to date. Its latest illusion, six and five, is not going to work either. It cannot simply superimpose six and five on social programs and expect it to make a bad program good or an expensive program reasonable and satisfactory.
I could address fiscal policy at length, but I will restrict my remarks to pension programs. It is safe to assume that all three Parties seated in the House support the concept of a minimum standard of income for all senior citizens, yet poverty persists in the country. Over 61 per cent of single persons over age 65 live in poverty, and about 14 per cent of families headed by persons over 65 are poor. In 1981, 3.7 million Canadians were below the poverty line, a figure which has not changed since 1977 in spite of the introduction of the spouse's allowance and enrichment of the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
While family allowance payments decrease annually as our birthrate declines and the population ages, this gain is more than offset by the 3.3 per cent compound annual growth rate of the senior citizen population. The substantial movement of women in the labour force where they may contribute to the Canada Pension Plan and private sector pensions, as well as
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
the growth of personal savings among new retirees, will help keep down the cost of tax-supported income security programs in the years ahead. However, to break the persistent hold of poverty on such a large percentage of our elderly and to guarantee a decent standard of living for present and future pensioners, pension reforms must be made now.
We must give real incentives to save for retirement, incentives which will be fair to persons in all income brackets. Private pensions must also be encouraged with respect to portability, vesting, indexing and survivor's benefits. There are many ways to reconstruct the pension system, but one way we should not follow is to limit indexing of the basic Old Age Security pension to six and five per cent over the next two very difficult years.
Our seniors have given enough to this country. We will make their golden years a lamentable farce if we force them to join the front lines of restraint and to give even more. Our senior citizens have served. They should not be called on again. It is our turn to lead the attack, not theirs.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Bill C-131 that we are discussing tonight is an extremely important Bill. It marks a part of the history of our country that I think will cause a serious setback. We are talking about the situation of senior citizens in Canada and the situation they will have to face in the future. I feel this particular Bill will, in many cases, put our senior citizens into a situation that is worse than the one they know now.
First, I want to speak a little bit about the life of the elderly in other cultures. I think it is important Canadian people in general take a look at how we treat our senior citizens. This is important because it says something about the way we look at human dignity and the value of people.
I have travelled a bit during my life and I have seen different cultures. Interestingly enough, in many cultures, the oldest citizens are the ones who get the greatest respect. They are the ones the rest of society looks after in a very special way.
I have travelled to Africa and through many villages. These villages have very little in the way of modern convenience as we know it. Yet the senior citizens of those villages are kept in honour. People go about their daily tasks, but the senior citizens, the wisdom of the community, are held together and are looked after and cared for by the whole community.
For centuries the Chinese have respected the wisdom of the old. That is true today in their culture. Right now in Singapore, which is a booming modern city, modern apartment blocks are set up for a family, but the apartments themselves are always set up as an apartment and a half. The apartment has a place, not only for the family, but for senior citizens.
In Canada other cultural forms have developed even in my own lifetime. One great step forward has been the idea that a senior citizen gets a pension and a senior citizen can look

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
forward to some kind of secure income. I can remember as a boy the fear that old people had that there was no future for them, that they had nothing to look forward to at all except what used to be called the poor house. That was basically unfair. I congratulate this Elouse and all the people in Canada who worked over the years to bring about universal pensions for our senior citizens.
This Bill is a setback to the very idea that we had accepted as a people that our senior citizens should be looked after in a special way.
My riding is Saskatoon East. Saskatoon East has a unique situation. In my riding there are probably proportionately more elderly people than in any other riding in Canada. Saskatoon is a city in Saskatchewan, and Saskatchewan has a very interesting age pattern. Sixty or seventy years ago, in the early days, young people from all over the world came to settle in Saskatchewan. My father said that when he went West in 1912 to take up a homestead, there were no people there with white hair. Ele does not remember seeing anybody who was old. Everybody was young. The person who was 30 years of age was considered old. Most people were 20 or 21 years of age. Those people were the pioneers and formed the Province. They were the ones who broke the Prairie, built the homes, built the schools, made the roads and built the towns. These people aged together. Right now in Saskatoon East I believe we have 18 or 19 senior citizen homes. We have St. Ann's home, the Jubilee buildings and Cosmopolitan Court. We have all these different places which the citizens have set up. When 1 speak to this Bill, I speak representing a lot of people who will be affected directly by the cutback in their pension and the fact that their pension will not keep up with the cost of living. I believe that is a direct challenge to the dignity of each one of those people.
As a priest I have done pastoral work for 30 years. One of the things a priest does is to visit senior citizens. Anyone working in pastoral work will tell you that there is one thing you must do and that is to visit senior citizens. They are lonely people. Many of them live with fear. Each one of us as we get a little older and our hair gets a little whiter-and, Mr. Speaker, you know what I am talking about when I talk about white hair-has within himself the question of security. A person will ask himself "Plow and where am I going to end up?" Yet, when we have our health and are able to carry on our responsibilities, that note does not strike as hard as when we get to the point in our lives-and it will come for each and every one of us-of reaching old age.
There are many reasons why this time becomes a very difficult period for many people. First, there is the question of death, not your own death but the death of people around you. This creates a state of loneliness. One wonders where so and so is. They have died. Then you think of somebody else and you realize they have died. Family members have moved away. Perhaps there is the death of a spouse. People become lonely and fear sets in. A person asks himself: where and how am I going to die?
If a person is secure from the worry of finances, that removes one of the problems of the fear of growing old. However, in the Bill before us today that notion of pension that was worked for by parliamentarians, by civil rights leaders and by leaders of communities all over Canada is being challenged on a principle that I think is a false principle. It is flippantly called the six and five principle. This six and five formula was passed by this House months ago as a way of handling inflation. The Bill encompassing that was passed by the Liberal Government and supported by the Conservatives. The NDP was the only Party that said the principle was wrong. Once you have a principle, you must accept the facts that follow from that principle. If you accept the six and five formula as a way to solve the financial problems of the country, you must accept the difficulties that you are putting into the lives of every person on whom you force the six and five formula. Adding this on to the problems faced by the senior citizens, those who have given their lives to build up this country, is, I believe, basically wrong.
The Party over there, the Government, has just stopped speaking to the Bill. I think their Members must hang their heads in shame because they have to go back to their constituencies and tell their senior citizens what the Government is doing. Over here, our friends the Conservatives are saying this Bill is a terrible thing, but they bought the principle. When you buy the principle you stand responsible for the results. 1 think the people of Canada should understand and know about that.
Let me come again to the notion of this extra slicing away at the income as the cost of living rises is such that a person with lots of money does not notice it. However, if a person does not have a great deal of money and is just making ends meet, he or she does notice it. He is struggling not to become any poorer. He is suddenly finding that while the cost of living keeps going up, his income is being cut back a little at a time.
I am sure Members of Parliament have spoken to senior citizens in their constituencies. Some senior citizens do not always understand what these measures mean. They do not understand the meaning of OAS, GIS or CPP. All that it means to them is that they cannot buy a bottle of milk, a pair of shoes or pay their telephone bills. They are finding themselves in a situation of fear, loneliness and growing misery.
Tonight we are debating this Bill, which will probably be passed. There is no one from the media here to write about the effects of this Bill on senior citizens. The Bill is being split up so that there will be no continuous debate; we may debate it again in another two days. In this way people will not realize what is taking place. The poor senior citizens, the founders of this country, are slowly being ripped off. Their standard of living will become worse than it is today.
A recently published book which was written by a modern theologian discusses the whole question of healing and caring for those who are hurting. In his recent book called "Clowning
November 25, 1982

in Rome", Henri Nouwen writes about the question of hurting, the pain that senior citizens know. He says:
I often wonder if the sheer artificiality and ugliness with which many people are surrounded are not as bad or worse than their interpersonal problems. I have found this painfully true in ministry to the elderly. Many old people suffer from the ugliness of their environment. Much healing could be offered to older people by helping them to make their home and room a little more beautiful.
I have visited the homes of some senior citizens. 1 do not think many people would want to live in some of those homes, but that is all those senior citizens have. They have a few artifacts in their homes which remind them of their families. They may have, for example, photograph albums with pictures of their families. Some of these senior citizens have difficulty making their own meals and must rely on people to bring food to them. Because of their loneliness they sometimes have a pet, such as a kitten or a puppy, in their home as companions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to answer the Hon. Member's questions at the end of my speech.
The point I was trying to make before the Hon. Member rose concerns the difficulty these people have in finding a comfortable and human surrounding. At this time I would like to pay tribute to those who have built accommodations, particularly in my area of Saskatchewan, which are providing senior citizens with comfortable surroundings. Those people now have pleasant apartments to live in. However, I am concerned about those who must still try to make it on their own. They are looking for the more human surroundings which make their lives a little better than it otherwise would be.
I used the example of having a pet as a companion because I know of a senior citizen who lives alone because his wife has died and his family has moved away. Last year, at Christmas, he received a kitten from a friend. While this may not seem like an extravagant gift for people who have two cars and a summer cottage, this kitten meant that he had a companion to which he could be near when he previously had nothing else to keep him company.
As a result of the six and five program the incomes of these senior citizens will slowly be cut back so that they will not even be able to enjoy these little luxuries which make life bearable and a little more human for them. When we talk about the mechanisms of the six and five program, it seems to have a cold nothingness to it. However, when we discuss it in relation to day-to-day living of a senior citizen and the fact that their incomes will be cut back, we see how hard this program strikes at the very heart of the matter. I cannot repeat often enough the callousness that forced the Minister to introduce this legislation and put this burden on the back of our senior citizens.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The Minister has now said that the pensions are increasing rather than being cut back. However, that has been said to me by many senior citizens. They do not want to end their lives in failure. The fact that they are forced into living with tests, letting the world know that they are poor and have been a failure, it is inhuman. subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
What the debate is about today, and the challenge against our senior citizens, is the fact that they are not going to be able to live within their pensions as they would want to.
I will go back to this basic notion of security because pensions were introduced, and, again, I give complete credit to those who introduced them, who fought in this House and who argued for them and found a way to bring them in.
About 20 years ago when I was visiting in Mexico with my father, we came to the first town inside the Mexican border about noon. There were old women begging on the steps of the church for food, and they were dressed in rags. I have seen millions of people like that since, but it was a shock. My father was really, really struck by that, the fact that these people were begging for food to survive. When we got back on the bus, he said that if it were not for the old age pensions in Canada it would be the same there. He was not a great sociologist or an economist but he was able to identify the fact that pensions that had been fought for and won in this country were the only possible way of keeping old people from being beggars in the last part of their lives when they no longer have an income sufficient to provide decent living conditions.
On the question of the dignity of receiving a pension, I would just like to refer to Hansard where our good colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), on October 21, 1951-that was the day when you no longer needed a means test to get a pension-talked about the historic significance of that day when the old age pension law was free of the means test. When that happened dignity was restored to senior citizens. It did not require a test to see if you were so poor and such a failure in life that you had to be looked at like an experiment to see whether or not you should get enough to live on. That was an historic day, and it was a great and happy day in this country when that happened.
On October 26, 1979 the same Member, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, said:
Members of the older generation, the generation to which I am proud to belong, are not ashamed to be on a pension. They are glad to show their identification cards and be recognized as part of today's senior citizen group. This is largely because we went for the principle of universality, because we decided we ought not to give pensions to older people just because they were poor but because they are people, because they have played their part in building up the life of this country and deserve a pension in the years of their retirement.
That is the principle, the dignity and self-respect of each person, each senior citizen, without tests, without fear, to be respected and to receive an income when they are in their declining years that will give them frugal comfort at least, human dignity, and not with the fear that this will collapse around them and that they will be left ailing and hurting when they are old.
What I would like to do is just to conclude with a few last remarks, hoping that this Government will find a way to assist elderly people, particularly women, because the majority of our senior citizens are women. They are also the ones who, because of the situation that exists in our country, have the least means of being looked after at this time. I will not go
through the details of each particular change, and what each year will mean, dollar for dollar, except that it is getting less.
Our pensioners, the ones we are talking about tonight, are the people who have led the way in our country. They are the people who were the pioneers, the ones who sacrificed, the ones who faced the thirties, lived the depression, sufferred the sicknesses, the poverty, the bad, whatever you want to say about the depression. They were the ones who sent their sons off to war and waited out four years, not knowing whether or not their boys would come back. Many of them did not. They were the ones who endured that kind of suffering. They built up this country. Now when they get to their final years, when there is a little possibility of having complete security, this Bill is attacking that. This Bill is cutting back on their pensions. The over-all result of six and five in this year, next year, and the third year is that they will have less to live on than they have today, in proportion to what it costs to live. That is not right.
We have to be sure that the universality of the pension plan is for all of the senior citizens. It has nothing to do with what they have done in life. An important point to remember is that nobody in this House or in Canada can tell how they are going to end up. They may be millionaires today but they still may need the old age pension when they get to be that age. Nobody can say that they have security. That is not the way life is.
My last thought on the subject tonight goes back to the first idea I had, the question about the importance of the human rights and dignity of every Canadian. I will be voting against this Bill because I believe that the basic rights of the founders of this country, the senior citizens of this country, are being attacked tonight, being whittled away. I just feel unhappy that that is the way it is.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a question which the Hon. Member will be able to answer very quickly. I heard his speech tonight. I heard many speeches from the other side tonight. I cannot help but feel that they must not have read the Bill. My question to the Hon. Member is very simple.
First, is he aware that this Bill does not change anything with regard to the universality of our Old Age Pension?
