subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one cannot help but agree that the Minister of Finance has shown the same ability to count as he has shown with the nation's finances.
I wish to address a few remarks between questions to this Bill to amend the Old Age Security Act. By this Act the Liberal Government promises to limit the indexation of the basic Old Age Security Pension to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent for the year after. What does this mean in practical terms? It means that the Liberal Party has abandoned the

November 25, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
principle of equity and fairness which is inherent and basic to the indexation.
Let us talk about indexation for a minute so that we understand exactly what it is based on. It is a principle brought forward by the Progressive Conservative Party. During the early 1970s our Party could see what was happening to this country as a result of the economic policies of the Liberal Government. My colleagues of the day argued that it was not fair to the federal Government to benefit from inflation. We argue that personal income tax exemptions should be indexed upwards, adjusted annually to account for inflation. In other words, if a fair income tax exemption was $1,500 and inflation for the year was 10 per cent, the income tax exemption should be adjusted by $ 150.
The same principle applies to the old age pension. For example, the old age pension cheque in November 1982 is $246.92. If inflation continues to run at 10 per cent for the entire year, the cheque should be increased by the amount of inflation, in which case the people receiving the old age pension should get an additional $24.70 per month.
What has happened? The Liberal Party is forcing senior citizens to absorb the difference. That is why we do not have a great flock of Liberal backbenchers supporting this Bill. They left it to the Minister. She is "several", the Minister of Finance said. We do not see great hordes of Liberal backbenchers, who usually have speeches prepared by the Department, putting those speeches forward so they can be included in their "Householder". Who wants an infamous speech as part of a "Householder?" The backbenchers are close enough to the line as it is, and this is going to sink them.
During the course of debate there have been some comments from my colleagues to the left about our Party voting for the principle of restraint. We did that. We believe in restraint. In July we supported the Government. You might ask why. Because after two and a half years of wallowing in indecision, of increased spending, of increased deficit, after two and a half years, realizing what a mess was created, the former finance minister brought in restraint. But should we really say it was two and a half years, or should we go back to the late 1960s when this Party gave the St. Lawrence Seaway pilots 30 per cent and started the avalanche? That is what started the precedent, and Canadians have paid for it ever since with inflation. As Members of Parliament when this Party came to decide on that restraint Bill, we voted for restraint, and everyone knows what the NDP voted for. They voted to retain the salary increases which they wanted.
When I went home for the summer the people I met on the street asked me why the NDP voted against the restraint. Why did they vote against cutting their increases to six per cent? I would have liked to be able to explain to the people because every so often there is one or two NDP supporters out of thousands. I would have liked to be able to say something other than, I am sorry, but my NDP colleagues voted to retain their salary increase. And they know darn well that is exactly
why they voted against that Bill. I do not want any of my Liberal colleagues to sit there smugly as if they had something to do with the restraint Bill. They know that restraint Bill came from Coutts, Davey and Axworthy. At least on our side of the House we had an opportunity to decide how we would vote on the Bill, whereas the sheep in the backbenches of the Liberal Party just did what they were told to do.
Let me say something about inflation because it is the very basis of what this Bill is all about. The inflation rate in March 1980 was 9.3 per cent. The Government worked it up to 13 per cent in July, 1981. Then it came up with the new idea to get it down, and this was called a recession. It worked on the recession and it has now got that recession right where it wants it. Now it has inflation down to 10 per cent. And what has happened to the prices that senior citizens are dealing with today? Pork prices have gone up 20.5 per cent. The purchasing power of the 1971-dollar is now 37 cents. Food prices have risen by 215 per cent. Housing costs have risen by 163 per cent. The 1981 average annual inflation rate of 12.5 per cent, created by the Liberal Party, was the highest in 33 years. And it was this Party, Mr. Speaker, that came into office by promising Canadians that it would not increase the price of gasoline.
I remember campaigning against my opponent in Simcoe North who promised the people, "No, sir, we will not increase the price of gasoline by 18 cents". He was right. He was telling the truth, which is unusual for a Liberal candidate. The Government did not increase the price by 18 cents. That was just a stop along the way. An interesting point, Mr. Speaker, is that we will have the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) gracing the riding of Simcoe North on December 3. He is having a soiree at $100 a ticket. He has the nerve to come to my riding, a riding that has faced an increase in the price of gasoline of 91 cents, for a $ 100-ticket soiree. Let me tell you, there will not be too many citizens on old age pensions who we are going to see at that soiree.
The other night the "several" speakers for the Liberal Party, otherwise known as the Minister of National Health and Welfare, (Miss Begin) made the opening speech, and it was a sad affair. This once proud Minister, humbled by her rejection of the senior citizens of Canada, came into this House and rejected everything she ever said in defence of senior citizens. This once proud champion of the poor and the downtrodden gave up, surrendered and backed off. I quote from Hansard of November 18, 1982 at page 20799. Here is what she said:
After all. we know that we cannot give any guarantees to pensioners that others will join them in the fight against inflation-
It was not the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who was over in France fighting inflation on $172,000 of the taxpayers' money. The Minister said, and this is a good one, and I quote from Hansard at page 20799 and 20800:
-and all pensioners will receive more in 1983 or in 1984 than in this current year, 1982.
That is unmitigated gall. My mother used to say, "That person has the nerve of a canal horse." and it takes nerve to
November 25, 1982

tell this House that the pensioners of Canada are going to get more money when she has turned her back on indexation.

I want to tell the Minister what is happening out in the real world, and I have a letter from one of my constituents, which reads as follows:
I am writing this protest, the indexing at 6 per cent of my, and many others, retirement pensions. I have been very grateful my pension has been indexed at the cost of living index. My wife and I both receive the basic old age pension which is also being indexed at 6 per cent-
The writer goes on to say that they have always been glad to receive these pensions. The letter goes on to say:
- but now we are wondering if it pays to try to be self-supporting. My wife also has a partial Canada Pension as she worked till the age of 65. I would be very grateful if you would express your opposition of this in your capacity as ... (my Member of Parliament).
These people are out there. That is what this Government refuses to acknowledge. That is why you do not have these kinds of speeches from the Liberal backbenches. But I would like to take you back to a speech the Minister made on April 20, 1982, in which she said:
We have no intention of changing the 'rules of the game'. We want to maintain indexing of the Old Age Security Pension and the Supplement every three months, and to retain the universality of the basic OAS pension.
What a difference six months makes in the approach and the rules of the game as seen by the Minister. And does the Minister wonder why the Canadian people do not believe the comments which she makes on universality? We have had a "bad-cop/good-cop" routine from the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Health and Welfare. The Minister of Finance says we are looking at universality. The Minister of Health and Welfare says we are not looking at universality. Who can believe what story? Which one is true?
Just before I left to come over here tonight, I found the final insult, the final backdown from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Minister is so ashamed of what she has done that she now has a new Act. She is so ashamed of what has happened to the Old Age Security Act under her authorship, she is now going to change it. It is now going to be the Senior Citizens' Benefits Act. The Minister just cannot live with what she has done to the security of old age pensioners. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this Party believes that a deal is a deal, and because the Government made a deal with the old age pensioners of this country and told them it would index their pensions to the rate of inflation, that deal must be kept. That is why we are voting against this Bill, because we believe that when you tell the people something, you must follow through with your word.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
This legislation is penalizing 1.2 million senior citizens who receive the Old Age Security pension and who presently do not qualify for either a full or partial Guaranteed Income Supplement. Based on an inflation rate of 10 per cent, each one of those 1.2 million senior citizens will be shortchanged and cheated by the Liberal Party of Canada to the tune of $290 over the next two years. Many of those people have incomes of slightly over $8,900 a year and are ineligible for the annual Guaranteed Income Supplement. That $290 means a great deal to those people. This Liberal legislation penalizes them, and penalizes elderly married couples with incomes just over $15,000. They lose $580 over the next two years.
It is about time that the Liberal Government lived up to the deal it made to index old age pensions. It said to the elderly of Canada: we want you to keep pace with inflation. Well, this Bill breaks that deal. This Liberal Government wants to make the old age pensioners of Canada suffer, and it is about time that it got out of office so that people and Parties who believe in their word can take over and give all Canadians a fair deal, not the kind of treatment they have been getting from the Liberal Government.

These people are below the poverty line, yet we have these two ministers rising and saying it is not true, these people will not lose. I would like to remind the Ministers that not all these people live in downtown Montreal where prices might be lower. They do not live in downtown Toronto,
Calgary or Winnipeg. Some of them live in isolated communities where milk is close to $2 a quart. Some of them are living in communities where bread runs $1 a loaf. Some people live in very high-cost communities. What do we say to those pensioners who cannot survive on what they have now? Do we tell them we are going to ride on their backs because the Government implemented a six and five program for the benefit of everyone and to help it get out of the economic mess it has created? It is absolutely sickening, Mr. Speaker, that in the year 1982 we would move in on the old people of this country who receive Old Age Security and tell them that we are going to take away some of their-

They did not have unemployment insurance as a safety net when they were out of work. They could not depend on social assistance and welfare to help them when they were unemployed. They had to grub with their own two hands. It brings tears to their eyes when they tell of the poverty they experienced while raising their children and launching them into the world.
I cannot imagine any Government, no matter how strapped for cash, attacking the Old Age Security payment. I cannot fathom that in this day and age. We are attacking the people who built this country and made it what it is today, so that we can all prosper.
We have many universities today and we have become the best educated population in the world. That did not happen because the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Health and Welfare brought in their short-sighted, terribly restrictive, theft policies. It happened because our senior citizens, those who came to this country as immigrants and those born here, suffered hardship, privation, depression, a drought on the Prairies and went without so that their children could eat. They built a nation. Today we are saying to them "We want you to sacrifice some more. You have not sacrificed enough."

We all know that there are elderly people and senior citizens whose lives have been shortened because of the privation they suffered and the struggles they had when they were young. We know that they did not get the nutrition they needed, and now we are denying it to them in their twilight years.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to oppose this Bill because I think it is one of the most unjust Bills that even this Government has devised so far.
I was a little shocked at the intervention made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Schroder). In the style of Liberal Members opposite, he did not choose to make a speech as a speech, but rather to question the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) and say that only $29 is to be taken away from pensioners next year.
I am surprised that the Hon. Member would choose to make that point. I think he is a man of even more experience than I, so he must know that $29 is not much when you have it. It is peanuts to anyone with an income of $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 per year. For someone earning the salary that the Hon. Member and I do, $29 is, perhaps, the price of a taxi to and from the airport. It is not much, it is hardly noticeable; neither the Hon. Member nor I would notice if $29 more were taken from our annual incomes. Surely the Hon. Member knows that the people who depend entirely upon the Old Age Security or the Old Age Security plus the GIS are in a very different situation. This $29 can mean almost one streetcar trip both ways per week through the year-one visit per week to a son or daughter, or one visit per week to a store which is more than walking distance away, one visit per week to go to some kind of free entertainment provided for senior citizens. It would be almost the price of a quart of milk per week. If the Hon. Member thinks that people on senior citizen incomes
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
have plenty of money for streetcars and milk, then I do not know where he has been living these last few years or who he has been living among. Certainly he has not been in touch with the people who live in the Spadina riding and in downtown Toronto.
If he had visited the streets of Spadina, if he had visited some of the rooming houses in downtown Toronto, if he had visited some of the old houses which have been maintained for years and years-in fact some of them have been maintained for 30 and 40 years-by one couple or perhaps the survivor of one couple, he would have a different picture. He would see people who are very thrifty, people who will scrub and clean their places in order to maintain the old wood of which their homes were built 100 years ago. He would see people who do minute repairs on their houses with their own hands, people who would not dream of having the money to hire someone to do the repairs. He would see people who still repair and make their own clothes for the same reason. He would see the remnants of half a dozen different waves of immigrants who entered Canada through downtown Toronto. Some of them moved on, some of them stayed there. Some of them have lived within a few blocks all their lives. These are the people who built the City of Toronto. I do not mean this only figuratively.
I am talking about construction workers who built buildings with their own hands.
I am talking about the cleaning women who clean the magnificent office towers every evening when the beautiful people have gone home. They come in and clean these expensive offices mostly for a minimum wage. They spend five hours an evening every weekday night cleaning these buildings and coming home about midnight, while their husbands, if they are lucky, have to get up at five o'clock to go to construction jobs. If they are not lucky, the husbands are out of work. These women may be the sole support of the family. I am talking about other women who have maintained the needle trade in Spadina for generations. They still maintain and manufacture much of the clothing we use in Canada. Again, many of them are the sole support of their families at this time of unemployment.
If he spent time among these people, he would understand that when they reach the age of senior citizens they have not been able to save very much. They were paying for their houses. They were raising their childen. Yes, they tried to save. Probably their first savings went to pay the mortgage. Yes, they tried to save more than that, but inflation got far ahead of them. What they were able to save, what they were able to put in insurance policies or pension plans, does not amount to a hill of beans for many of them. As I say, these are the people who built our city. In fact, they are the people who built our country. They built it with hard work. They were not allowed in our so-called free market system to do much saving. This is why they still live in western downtown Toronto. They did not make it to the mansions of Forest Hill or the richer parts of

November 25, 1982

North York or Mississauga. They are still living where they brought up their children.
Many of these people had little opportunity to learn English or French. They learned what was called construction English, at least the men did. Perhaps the women had less opportunity than even their husbands to learn it. To follow the complications of the language of legislation is impossible for them. They come to my office to ask what a government form concerning their pensions means. They ask whether it means that they will get this much or that much money; they do not understand it. These people are doubly shut out from understanding what the Government across the way is doing to them this evening.
Not only has the Government made successfully sure that very little goes into the media, it has chosen to chop the debate into little bits-one day here, one day there and one day another time. This is so that there will be no impact upon public understanding. The thousands and thousands of people about whom I am speaking in western downtown Toronto are further shut out by the language barrier imposed upon them by the conditions of their work when they came to help build this country. Therefore, they are among the weakest and most defenceless people in Canada. They are not the weakest in work, in courage, in thrift or in morality, but the weakest in ability to know what the Government is doing to them and to protest against it.
Their work has been taken from them. For the greater part, most of them were directed to put their work into somebody else's property, factory, store or construction company. They gave their working time at whatever was the price which could be negotiated. Their work has now been taken from them. They own no means of production.
Aside from their wages they were given the promise of a decent pension in their old age. They were told not to worry about it if they did not own farms as did their fathers or perhaps their grandfathers at home. They were told not to worry about it if they did not own a store or had to sell their home or business because of rising property taxes. They were told not to worry if they did not own a factory, a big daily newspaper or part of an oil company. They were told not to worry because they had a pension. Furthermore, now that inflation is galloping they are told that their pensions will be indexed so as to keep pace with prices. They are told that they will not get rich but that at least they will remain at a certain level of buying power.
We heard some yipping and chirping from across the way on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) about how old people will get more dollars next year. That was a very cynical and misleading statement to put forward. The Minister knows well that getting more dollars next year is not the point. She knows well that they will buy less with the dollars they get next year than with the dollars they get this year.

We do not hear that bragging now, and for good reason. The prices which this federal Government administers, as well as the prices which the provincial Governments administer, are not coming anywhere near a 6 per cent increase.
The Government had the choice to intervene in the setting of the prices of fuel and gasoline. The Government had the choice to intervene in certain cases of rents. But in those and other Government administered prices, it has simply scorned, derided and utterly rejected any idea of holding prices down to 6 per cent increases. And yet the Minister has the gall to suggest that these pensioners next year will have greater spending power than they have this year. The Minister keeps on yipping, "More dollars," but she knows that more dollars will buy less because her Government has decreed that the prices it administers will go up not 6 per cent but 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent.
The majority of the working people I know around Spadina have not had the opportunity to participate in strong company pension plans. They have not had the opportunity to pile up savings in private pension plans that were strong enough to stand against our galloping inflation. Therefore, they are going to be in trouble next year. For the most part they do not know it yet, but I know that beginning not January 1, maybe not even February 1, but soon after that they will be coming to my office and asking me what has happened to their pensions. The message will begin to sink through to them that many of them will not be getting a pension that will keep up with price increases.
The Government has chosen to cut the incomes of roughly half the pensioners. In other words, it will cut the incomes of those who are on Old Age Security only. It will cut their real buying power. The Government is not trying to hold down prices but is willing to pass a law to renege on what it promised those people. The Government is willing to pass a law to take away what it guaranteed to people over past years and for the future. For what? What is so important, crucial and overwhelming that the Government feels compelled to cut the incomes of some of our poorest people in the country?
According to the Government, it will get an average of $29 from each person. There is a little over one million of these pensioners. It means that the Government will take in the range of $30 million from the pensions. The Government will take from those pensioners $30 million, which is about one-tenth of 1 per cent of the deficit which the Government is running up. The Government has run up a deficit which we are told sometimes is $25 billion, sometimes $26 billion and we even hear it is $27 billion.
The Government would have to take one thousand times as much as it is taking from the pensioners to clear that deficit.
November 25, 1982

Of course, the Government is taking money from others as well. The Government is not seriously cutting back on its expenditures on wasteful causes. It is clear the Government does not need that $32 million so desperately. The only possible reason that I can see why the Government has chosen to undermine the incomes of half the pensioners in Canada is that this is part of the Government's long-range strategy to do away with the principle of universality. The Government has chosen some of the weakest and most inarticulate people in the country-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Parliamentary Secretary is having difficulty understanding this point, I will explain it if he will allow me. What has been done is to say that pensioners are now to be divided into two groups. One group is to have this right of a guaranteed pension with indexation called into question. No longer will this group get full indexation. Indexation will be done on the basis of a means test, the means test used for the GIS. In other words, the Old Age Security pension will now be tied in with the GIS. It was not tied in before. The Old Age Security was independent and guaranteed, given to people as a right. Now it will no longer be given to them as a right. Now they must crawl and prove, as my colleague the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) said, that they are failures in order to be given the full indexed pension that was previously guaranteed for them. That is a direct attack on the principle of universality.
I can understand why the Minister of National Health and Welfare is so sensitive about this, if, as is very likely, she was on the losing end of a battle within Cabinet and she lost out to the man who is now the Minister of Finance. She would feel very sensitive about that. She feels doubly sensitive when she has to carry the blame for what he forced upon her. I can even understand her using some unparliamentary language during a speech before supper.
The fact is very clear that the Cabinet has decided to undermine the principle of universality. It does not have the courage to do it openly. A few speeches have been made here and there. The Minister of Finance said some things which he has qualified and he has danced around and said, "I do not really want to do that." But the way of introducing and trying to legitimize their idea is to begin with some of the weakest people in the country by taking away the right of a guaranteed Old Age Security pension on the ground that these people have
Adjournment Debate
not proved that they are failures. That is a direct attack upon the principle of universality. We will see more of that from this same Government as long as the people of this coutry let the Liberals stay in office. This is a shameful Bill which the Government has put forward. It is shameful that the Progressive Conservative Party voted for that in June.

They would like to wipe it out from the minds of the old age pensioners whom they have helped to cheat. The old age pensioners will not forget. subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-IMPACT ON PETROCHEMICAL PROJECTS. (B) FUTURE OF MEGAPROJECTS. (C) MINISTER'S ACTIONS
NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-IMPACT ON PETROCHEMICAL PROJECTS. (B) FUTURE OF MEGAPROJECTS. (C) MINISTER'S ACTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 17, and again on November 19, as reported at pages 20734 and 20820 respectively, of Hansard, I raised questions with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) and the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) pertaining to the disastrous effects of the National Energy Program upon the petrochemical industry.
I think it is summarized quite appropriately in a recent Globe and Mail article entitled "Feedstock Prices Crucial to Petrochemicals' Future". It states:
Unless the federal Government soon recognizes petrochemicals as a manufacturing sector with a distinct feedstock price structure, the Petrosar and Petromont plants in eastern Canada may be partly closed, says Norman Kissick, President of Union Carbide Canada Ltd. of Toronto.
It goes on to say:
The petrochemicals industry is in a period of severe crisis, he said in an interview. "There is no time for further debate."
The article goes on to elaborate on the situation in other parts of the country as well.

November 25, 1982
Adjournment Debate
This is an industry in which Canada, with our abundance of natural gas as a feedstock, should easily have been a world leader. It is an industry which depends upon natural gas as its major feedstock and natural gas has to be competitive in order for the petrochemical industry to compete in the international marketplace.
This Government, however, through its imposition of the natural gas and gas liquids tax, the Canadian Ownership tax and the petroleum gas and revenue tax, has imposed crippling taxes upon the feedstock, namely natural gas. As a result of this, the basic feedstock price has been driven up at least 25 per cent higher than the competition from American competitors. The totality of this tax amounts to $1.05 per thousand cubic feet of natural gas. When it is worked out on the balance sheet, it amounts to 35 per cent of the netback revenue of petrochemical companies.
In 1978, this federal Government embarked upon a program of studying the various industrial sectors in this county. The 1978 task force on petrochemicals said that, as a minimum position, the Canadian Government should ensure that the cost of feedstocks and energy used in the manufacture of petrochemicals does not exceed the cost on the U.S. Gulf Coast. We know that as a result of the imposition of this very burdensome tax Canada is now in a non competitive position in so far as its feedstock is concerned.
This is what some people in the petrochemical industry are saying, and I will quote from the OilWeek Magazine of September 20, 1982 which says:
Robert L. Pierce, Executive Vice-President of Nova, an Alberta Corp., told a conference earlier this year that the burden of the natural gas and gas liquids tax, plus the Canadian ownership charge, had a substantial effect on the cost of manufacturing ethylene and represented about $20 per tonne, or about 11 per cent of the plant gate price, of methanol. Clifford Mort, former Chairman of Dow Chemical Canada, said the taxes have added about 50 per cent to the variable cost of natural gas based ethane and a 'staggering 20 per cent increase' in the total cost of ethylene.
It goes on to say:
'It seems ludicrous' Mort said, 'that one of the few industries in Canada that had the prospect of competing effectively in world markets and whose expansion is based on large surpluses of supplies of natural gas should suddenly have a questionable future as a result of upfront taxes.'
Meanwhile, price is also a worry for petrochemical manufacturers in eastern Canada which use oil based feedstocks to produce not only ethylene, but the higher olefins and aromatics which are not available from the manufacture of ethylene from ethane.
As well, Mr. Lapalme of the Union Carbide Corporation said that Canada is pricing itself out of the petrochemical business and parts of the industry are desperately looking for ways to survive. That puts the issue into context.
This industry base is dependent very largely upon exports. Eighty-five per cent of the end product is export. The selling price is set in the international marketplace so it must be competitive. It cannot pass these additional taxes on to the consumer.
One of the ironies of these taxes is that they are imposed on revenues and not on profits, so the Government has turned
previously profitable tax-paying companies into losers. We all know that this Government supports losers. The result is that today there are at least a dozen petrochemical plants worth $4.5 to $5 billion on hold. They will not go ahead, they will not be developed unless there is some relief from these taxes.
Alberta Gas Chemicals Limited indicated in a report recently, and I quote:
The taxes have reduced Alberta Gas Chemicals from a profitable tax-paying Canadian corporation to a projected loss in 1983. The company can survive the world-wide recession and the legislated increases in natural gas prices but not both of these plus the federal Government's taxes on natural gas.
The result of these taxes is the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs, and the spin-off benefits that would be associated with other industries.
Alberta Gas Chemicals Limited is now in the process of engaging in a joint venture with a New Zealand interest because of the feedstock, because the better tax treatment is such that they will then be able to manufacture their product and compete in the international marketplace. I say that is shameful.
No one is denying the fact that the economy is in an over-ail recession, but the petrochemical industry is burdened by the recession, by the increase in energy prices, but primarily by the prohibitive tax structure. I urge the Minister and the Government to reconsider their position and make some amendments so that this industry can develop and continue to provide the jobs and the wealth this country needs.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-IMPACT ON PETROCHEMICAL PROJECTS. (B) FUTURE OF MEGAPROJECTS. (C) MINISTER'S ACTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did like the remarks of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), some of which were excellent in my opinion. We too on this side can make very good comments. As you can see, there are always two sides to everything. Let us start with the situation in the petrochemical industry. Along the Gulf Coast in the United States they are faced with the same problem as we are in Canada because many plants are closing down; the same thing happens in Japan, where three plants have closed down in large petrochemical complexes. Europe is experiencing similar difficulties, which goes to prove that this is really a world-wide phenomenon, a direct result of the economic recession and above all of the oil glut which forced OPEC to bring their price down.
Now let us look at the problem in Canada, keeping in mind that I only have three minutes to answer this question. Various businesses now in operation have been created in relation to megaprojects, and despite the cancellation of some of these projects, others are still showing some positive results. The Department is currently carrying out new surveys in the petrochemical field and, in connection with the megaprojects which were under construction and those which are planned
November 25, 1982

over the next ten years, it is expected there will be 200 direct surveys related to petroleum, and the funds invested in those 200 surveys might generate investments of up to $250 billion.
Here are a few actual examples of job creating projects in the energy sector. Several of them are now being carried out and others will be completed within the next ten years, including some which are now under way and others still in the planning stage: $2 billion for the development of the Venture-Sable Island gas deposit, $3 billion for the Western-LNG project, $3 billion for coal mining in northeastern British Columbia, $1 billion for the Norman Wells oil field and pipeline, and, in the past six months, the signed exploration agreements with respect to the Scotian Slope and Shelf, near Sable Island, and, in the Beaufort Sea, the upper expanses of the Arctic, and Davis Strait, $250 billion in investments which are expected to create quite a number of new jobs. All those projects are still in the planning stage and will be carried out over the next ten years.

subtopic: PORTS-REMOVAL OF GRAIN ELEVATOR FROM PORT OF MONTREAL. (B) OFFER TO PURCHASE ELEVATOR
PORTS-REMOVAL OF GRAIN ELEVATOR FROM PORT OF MONTREAL. (B) OFFER TO PURCHASE ELEVATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my part in the debate this evening arises out of a question I directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on November 9 concerning terminal No. 1 or Annex No. 1 in the old Port of Montreal. The question arose out of an answer the Minister gave to one of his colleagues on the Government side. He was asked whether this Port and this Annex would be maintained to enable producers to truck grain into a terminal rather than be denied that privilege. Although the question was asked on November 9, the discussion on Annex No. 1 or the old terminal began on March 28, 1982.
A wholly-owned Canadian company, Allstate Grain, offered to purchase grain elevator No. 1 from the National Harbours Board. The National Harbours Board reply was that this facility would be turned over to Public Works Canada and would be demolished. The Allstate Grain Company, a wholly-owned Canadian company could not quite understand why this would happen. Over the last year it had purchased a Government terminal in the City of Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan which it operates without Government subsidies. It continues to operate that for the benefit of producers of grain in that area. It wished to do this for the producers and shippers of grain in the Port of Montreal.
The rationale for the destruction of this terminal and facility does not make a lot of sense. It will cost the taxpayers of Canada millions of dollars to remove it. In reply to my question, the Minister said there is:
-an organization which is very anxious to take hold of that land, I said at the time, and I repeat now, that there are other facilities available to Quebec farmers who want to deliver their grain by truck. They can go to Sorel, to Quebec City, and also to Trois-Rivieres.
I have had communication from the Minister of Transport, as have other Members of this House. We do not find it all that strange for the Minister to suggest that people who want to use this facility travel the distances that he recommends;
Adjournment Debate
168 miles to Quebec City, 50-some miles to Sorel and a little under 100 miles to Trois-Rivieres.
I do not find that strange when the same Minister of Transport informed the people in Arelee, Saskatchewan that there was room in an elevator at Wilkie, 165 miles away. He expected people to deliver their grain there because their line had been removed.
To carry on with the rationale for the destruction of this facility, it was not to build a new facility or improve the shipping capability in the Port of Montreal. It was to build a promenade, to beautify the City of Montreal. That is all very well, but it is to the detriment of the grain producers of Canada and the grain growers in the Quebec region. While all this took place beginning March 28, or March 31, on through May, there was an article in the Montreal Gazette of June 14, and I quote:
The National Harbours Board and Bunge of Canada Ltd. have agreed to invest $3.5 million each to renovate Annex No. 1 of the Port of Quebec's oldest grain elevator-
Work is expected to begin this summer on the elevator, which is operated by Bunge.
Bunge is not a Canadian company.
By the spring of 1983, unloading capacity of grain carried from western Canada by railroad is expected to increase by between 12 to 20 cars an hour.
This improvement should increase grain elevator capacity at the Port of Quebec by 500,000 tonnes a year-
A study made by Cansilo Ltd. last February recommended that Annex No. 1 serve as the receiving area and warehouse of export grain, besides continuing to be a winter warehouse for grain.
That winter warehouse, Mr. Speaker, is very important to the grain producers of western Canada because since 1979, under the initiative of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), grain was transported from Thunder Bay by rail to the ocean ports, stored and shipped overseas, which has greatly increased the export of grain from western Canada.
But the point is, and I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) will be answering, on June 14 there was an announcement of an investment of $7 million by the National Harbours Board and Bunge of Canada Ltd. into renovating Annex No. 1; a study was carried out by Cansilo Ltd. last February recommending that investment, so why have the National Harbours Board and the Department of Public Works decided to destroy the elevator and remove that facility which has benefited, and could benefit, the grain producers in the Quebec area and western Canada? It seems there is more at stake and more important things than the movement of grain. It happens to be a promenade in the old Port of Montreal. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to answer these questions, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PORTS-REMOVAL OF GRAIN ELEVATOR FROM PORT OF MONTREAL. (B) OFFER TO PURCHASE ELEVATOR
speechtext:
I do not know why Hon. Members are whistling. I apologize for the formal attire, Mr. Speaker, but I just returned from the National Harbours Board Police dinner.

November 25, 1982
Adjournment Debate
There are not too many Canadians who know that the National Harbours Board Police is the oldest police force in Canada, having its origins in the Port of Quebec in 1837. I think it is fitting that tonight I am answering a question of the Hon. Member pertaining to the Port of Montreal.
The closure of grain Elevator No. 1 at the Port of Montreal is an integral part of two major expenditure programs; the Vieux Port Project, and the efforts to bring grain operations at the Port up to the state-of-the-art technology. The phasing out of Elevator No. 1 was decided in conjunction with the desire of the City of Montreal to restore the historical Vieux Port area. The significance of this area can be measured by the fact that this is where Jacques Cartier landed almost 450 years ago, in 1535. I know many of my colleagues from the Montreal area, as well as the grain producers in Quebec, are very anxious to get on with this restoration.
The second factor in phasing out the elevator was that, having been built in the 1920s, it did not warrant the major capital expenditures required to bring it up to present standards of efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It was estimated that $8 million would be required to make the necessary improvements in safety standards alone, not to mention other improvements. Instead, it was decided to expand Elevator No. 4, built in 1963. This expansion and modernization is now well under way, and is expected to be completed early in 1983, at a total cost of $8.9 million.
The benefits from this project far outweigh the loss resulting from the closure of Elevator No. 1. Number 1 has a storage capacity of 112,020 metric tons, whereas No. 4. will have a storage capacity of 265,000 metric tons when the current work is completed, compared to the 154,020 metric tons it had previously. Number 1 has a throughput capacity of 1,500 tonnes per hour, compared with 3,600 tonnes per hour for Number 4 upon completion, considerably more than the previous combined throughput capacity of the two elevators.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE-APPLICATION TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY LAY-OFFS. (B) NECESSITY FOR NOTIFICATION
CANADA LABOUR CODE-APPLICATION TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY LAY-OFFS. (B) NECESSITY FOR NOTIFICATION
speechtext:
I rise tonight to further my question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) which has to do with application to the British Columbia Telephone Company regarding lay-offs. I stated, as reported at page 20740 of Hansard of November 17, 1982:
Last summer the British Columbia Telephone Company announced it was laying off about 1,800 people. These people were laid off without adequate notice as required by the Canada Labour Code-
I was very disappointed, Mr. Speaker, with the answer the Minister of Labour gave to my questions last week concerning the Government's lay-off legislation and regulations. In response to both my questions the Minister told me that the matter was before the courts. I can only think that he was not aware of the problem, because the answer he gave was not true.
It is true that one question is before the courts. Last August a British Columbia Supreme Court judge ruled that part of Section 30 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Regulations was ultra vires, and that matter had been sent to the B.C. Court of Appeal. But that was not what I asked about. I asked about amendments to Section 30 of the Labour (Standards) Regulations which the Government passed after its other regulations had been struck down. These new regulations are not before the courts.
I wanted to know why the Government had passed new regulations which took away from workers and unions their protection against lay-offs. In other words, Bill C-78 had provisions that where more than 50 workers are laid off at one time they must be given 16 weeks notice. The Minister dodged that question by pretending it was before the courts.
My second question had absolutely nothing to do with the courts. Under the regulations an employer is able to lay-off up to 50 people from an industrial establishment without the protection of lay-off legislation being offered to laid off workers. In the case of Bell Canada in Quebec, that company is trying to weasel out of those provisions by doubling its number of industrial establishments from about 35 to about 70. That means it could lay-off 49 people in each of the 70 establishments without offering any protection. It has already said it is laying off about 400 people in Quebec and not offering them proper notification of lay-offs. So I ask the Minister if it was his intention to let companies like Bell use the legislation in this way, and if not, what was he going to do about it?
I want to emphasize that the matter is not before the courts, but the jobs of many workers are on the line. These workers deserve an answer. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will not try to stick them with the same phony answer the Minister gave me last week.

speakeroldname: Mr. Antonio Yanakis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE-APPLICATION TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY LAY-OFFS. (B) NECESSITY FOR NOTIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish indeed to thank the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) for raising this very important question. The question was why a new amendment to Section 30 was passed when a B.C. Supreme Court judge had already ruled part of that Section ultra vires.
The question seems to imply that a new regulation, Section 30(1 )(f) of the Canada Labour (Standards) Regulation, was passed after the B.C. Supreme Court judge ruled a similar Section, Section 30(1 )(d), to be ultra vires. Section 30(1 )(f) had been under development since April 1982. It was processed through the various steps necessary for enactment and was approved by the Governor in Council on July 29, 1982, at which time it became law. It was published in The Canada Gazette on August 11, 1982.
The judicial decision on section 30(1) (d) was handed down by Mr. Justice Spencer of the B.C. Supreme Court on August 5, 1982, one week after the enactment of section 30(1 )(f). In
November 25, 1982

fact, therefore, the new regulation was in force prior to the court action referred to by the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker). The approximate juxtaposition of the court ruling on 30(1 )(d) and enactment of 30(1 )(f) was entirely a coincidence. The two events were unrelated.
Because the initial decision with respect to 30(1 )(d) is under appeal before the B.C. Supreme Court, Mr. Speaker, we are awaiting their decision before giving further consideration to
Adjournment Debate
Regulation 30. And, as the Minister pointed out the other day, when a decision is announced by the Court, we will proceed in light of that decision.
